speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks to put into effect the 1958, 1962 and 1963 promise of the Liberal party to allow the building, among other things, of a second trans-Canada highway. It seeks to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act to that end by permitting the act to speak in the plural rather than in the singular, as it is at the moment.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-78, to amend the Immigration Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF PERSONS RECOVERED FROM MENTAL ILLNESS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING STATUS OF PERSONS RECOVERED FROM MENTAL ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to make an amendment to the Immigration Act which will grant permanent status to people who have at some time in their lives suffered a mental illness. Under the present act if a person has ever suffered a mental illness he cannot have permanent status in this country. On the other hand, certain criminals after they have been rehabilitated are allowed permanent status. This amendment will allow people who have suffered from mental illness the same rights as criminals.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, June 20, consideration of a motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we rose last night I had made two points in connection with the budget. The first one concerned the increased tax exempt period for new mines in order to encourage industrial and mineral development in northern Canada, including that part of Canada below the 60th parallel. I also made the point that it is high time some consideration was given to increasing the basic income tax exemption for residents of northern Canada in order to stimulate the development of these areas of this country.
I want to pass now to a discussion of the effect that the 11 per cent sales tax on building material is going to have in the north. Since the passage of the National Housing


Act in 1935, and until 1957, in a period of some 22 years there were only two homes built in the Yukon under the National Housing Act. Obviously it was not working. As a result of amendments and enlargements made in that act by the previous administration to encourage home building, building has surged ahead in the north. I submit that building has a very direct bearing on the rapidity with which the north is going to develop. Well over 100 homes have been built in the Whitehorse area alone as a result of the enlarged provisions of the National Housing Act. I can tell the minister, without any doubt whatever, that the imposition of this 11 per cent sales tax on building materials will so affect house construction in the Yukon as to virtually bring it to a standstill. The 11 per cent tax is damaging enough in the southern areas of Canada when it is applied to home construction, and I think the minister will soon see how the number of starts will diminish as a result of this burdensome tax, but it is absolutely killing so far as home construction in the north is concerned. I would urge the minister to consider the suspension or removal of the sales tax on building materials in so far as these areas of Canada are concerned.
Certainly it is a tax that should not be imposed at all, because it is going to be so burdensome on those who are attempting to build their own homes in Canada that house construction will be seriously diminished indeed. I do not believe I am alone in these views, because some of the national press comment has been severely critical of the imposition of this tax. For instance, the June 15 issue of the Globe and Mail had this to say:
Look at the whole thing carefully, and it is clever, if not particularly scrupulous. Rather like a store that offers two articles for the price of one, having first thoughtfully doubled the price of the one.
This, of course, is a reference to the $500 bonus for winter home construction that the Minister of Labour announced the other day in the house. The Globe and Mail in the same issue went on to say:
It could work; but is it the kind of economic philosophy that is reassuring in a finance minister?
The president of Belcourt Homes in Montreal had this to say:
The manufacturers' 11 per cent sales tax on building materials will automatically bring with it a $700 to $1,500 increase in the price of new homes and knock a lot of small builders out of business.
I think we all agree that one of the needs of this country for many years has been the supplying of a sufficient number of homes in order to raise the standard of living of our citizens throughout the nation. I think

there cannot be any serious argument advanced but that some of the most aggressive measures in Canada's history were taken by the previous administration under the terms of the National Housing Act to bring about an accelerated home building program in Canada that has heretofore not been matched. It will certainly be difficult to equal the record for home building in the last five years. Surely we should be looking not toward the imposition of a tax that would curtail home building in Canada, as this one will, but rather toward incentives to build more homes. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance, perhaps in his desperation to find sources of revenue in order to pay for election promises, has had to penalize one of the areas of our economy that could least stand these penalties.
I want to pass now, Mr. Speaker, to a brief reference to the Carter commission on taxation. Perhaps as a result of representations made by my colleague from the Northwest Territories, I understand the commission will be sitting in Yellowknife, Whitehorse and Yukon. I believe the Whitehorse sitting is going to be on July 23. Perhaps, therefore, any further representations which people have in respect of taxation in the north can be brought before that commission and the minister might have an opportunity to consider them when the commission reports.
I wish to deal now with another sector of northern economy, that of the mining industry. The future of the north is essentially a mining future. However, I do intend to make a few remarks in order to set the record straight concerning the Dawson city festival and the tourist industry in the north. The mining economy in the north also is one which, if it is to develop at all, needs special incentives in order to induce risk capital to come to that area. Mining capital is high risk capital. It is capital that is invested at approximately a ratio of 20 to 1.
If we stop for a moment to consider, we will realize that before any mine can go ahead it has to develop a community; it has to develop housing, schools, roads and communications. If we consider for a moment the effect that the 11 per cent sales tax will have on the development of the mining industry, having regard to these facilities I mentioned, homes, schools, and the like, we can see immediately that this statute is going to reach its tentacles into this area to throttle or seriously set back the development of the mining industry in the north.
Instead of taxation measures such as these proposed in the budget, surely there should be measures which would, first of all, induce high risk capital, Canadian or foreign, to come
The Budget-Mr. Nielsen into the north, and measures which will encourage the development of mines. I see no such measures in this budget, despite the repetitive statements that were made by the present minister in his book "Troubled Canada". I suggest, in keeping with editorial comment, that Canada may be just as troubled after the budget as it was before.
One of the most important things in the north, of course, is communications, the building of roads and land lines. The establishment of communications is very essential to the development of the whole of the nation. Without adequate communications the Canadian west would not have developed. Similarly, without adequate communications the 40 per cent of Canada lying above the 60th parallel and the northern portions of the provinces will not be adequately developed. Under the last administration there was a very dynamic roads to resources and development roads program which encouraged the development of the resources throughout the whole of northern Canada, including the northern portions of the provinces. I do not see any mention at all of this in the budget; as a matter of fact I see a serious lack of reference to it in the current estimates.
I am told that one of the commitments the Prime Minister made while on a visit to Whitehorse was that when a Liberal government was elected a road would be constructed from Whitehorse to Skagway. This is what the Liberal candidate in my riding quoted the Prime Minister as having promised him, and it was one of the things on which he campaigned. I certainly hope this is so and that the Prime Minister and his government will construct that road to Skagway, because it will of course give us access to Tidewater through the Alaskan Panhandle and is essential to the development of our resources in the Yukon.
The Liberal candidate in my constituency also quoted his leader, the present Prime Minister, as promising that when a Liberal government was elected the Alaskan highway would be paved. There were no ifs, ands or buts about it, and as there is no indecision in this government I assume that the Alaskan highway paving program will be proceeded with immediately. However, I was rather disappointed not to see any reference in the budget to these projects. We, in the Yukon, would certainly like them to be proceeded with, at the earliest possible moment. We have no doubt whatever that the Prime Minister will adhere to his word and proceed with them with the least possible delay.
Mr. Speaker, before I proceed to a discussion of the festival matter I wish to say a

The Budget-Mr. Nielsen word about patronage. Before 1957, not affected by the tradition which seems to exist in Quebec and certain portions of the mari-times, I thought that the conduct of the previous Liberal administration in the Yukon was something less than fair in dealing with the disposition of public works and services to those who wished to perform them for the government. In some cases tenders were not called at all and in a good many other cases people were selected to carry out undertakings for the government because of their political partisanship. After 1957, quite apart from any feelings which I think existed (perhaps not exclusively in any one political party) with respect to patronage but because of a feeling that I did not think this was fair, I caused correspondence to be sent to all departments of government-any minister who sits opposite now may verify this simply by checking his departmental files-requesting that in all cases public works and services of all kinds should be called for by public tender.
I am very disappointed to see that despite six years under the Progressive Conservative administration, where the previous policy of patronage had been eliminated there has been a resurgence of his ugly and dishonest practice. I say that it is crooked; in fact I would say that it is corrupt, because all that it indicates is a pay-off to political friends for assisting a political party. Patronage is being employed once again in the Yukon territory in order to pay off political friends. I say to the government benches, let us get back to the fair practice of calling for tenders for all public works and services and completely eliminate this ugly practice of patronage. There is no reason for it, and in my view every Canadian has an equal right to bid for every public work or service that the government requires.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word about the Dawson city festival. I am very sorry to see that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is not in his seat, because these words are applicable to his department more than to any other; his departmental officials had a great deal to do with the planning of this festival. It has been referred to by the Secretary of State and sometimes parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance as one of the reasons for the deficit. I believe in his most recent remarks it was referred to by the Minister of Finance himself as a fiasco. Yet when I asked the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources on two separate occasions in this house to produce the other side of the picture in order to let the house judge on a fair basis, upon production of all the facts, he

refused to do so. I telephoned his office last week in order to obtain figures, and these have not been supplied to me.
It seems to me only fair to put on the record both sides of the picture. Certainly the festival suffered a deficit of $80,000, but I do not see any difference between the federal government bailing out the Dawson city festival to the tune of that figure, or even to the tune of much more, and what was done, if I recollect accurately, during the time Mr. St. Laurent was prime minister, when $250,000 was granted to the Stratford festival in order to bail it out, and this was matched by a like sum from the provincial government of Ontario.
I do not think it is wrong to invest in festivals if this is going to attract tourists to this country. Tourism from the United States to Canada last year produced a revenue of over $550 million; for the first time we had a favourable balance of tourist dollars with the United States. If it was wrong, surely the government of Ontario would not be going ahead with Upper Canada village to the tune of an investment of $2J million, and surely the federal government would not be going ahead with the restoration of Louisburg. The preliminary cost estimates of the partial restoration of Louisburg amount to over $10 million.
Mr. Speaker, an hon. member has just asked a question which I did not hear. I am told by my colleague that it referred to Canadian players appearing at the Stratford festival, and I am sure that not only Canadian players have appeared at that festival, as the hon. lady would know if she has ever attended it. Surely it cannot be wrong to invest over $2 million in Barkerville in British Columbia. The fact is that the Dawson city festival was a financial success if it is viewed not in terms of revenue from the festival itself but in the proper terms of including the revenue from those people who came to see the territory as a result of the festival being there.
I have here a summary that I managed to obtain, quite apart from the assistance of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, in connection with the festival. There were a total of 18,545 visitors to Dawson city during the festival. They chose Dawson city itself, quite apart from the Yukon. They all had to go through British Columbia and Alberta to get there. Six thousand of these visitors stayed in Dawson city an average of three days, 5,000 stayed an average of two days and 7,545 stayed an average of one day. The estimated daily expenditures per person is figured at $25, which would include accommodation, meals, tours, theatres,

gasoline and car maintenance. The estimated gross revenue for Dawson city alone was $888,625 as a result of the festival. The number of visitors in 1961 was estimated at between 6,000 and 8,000, almost three times as many as the usual number. A total of 3,904 cars came to Dawson during the period, and between July 1 and August 18 the average number of visitors per car was 2.5, totalling 14,510. The estimated tourist revenue from the festival was $1,200,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I regret to have to tell the hon. member that his time has expired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have had an opportunity to speak in this twenty sixth parliament. Some hon. members may recall that I had the honour of sitting briefly in the last parliament. At that time I did make my maiden speech. However, as the election was subsequently declared void ab initio, I wonder if I am now in the unique position of making my second maiden speech.
I should like to say it was a pleasant change to see the government bring in a budget, and I hope we have returned to this practice. No doubt an awful lot of the fussing and fuming we have heard from hon. members opposite stems from the fact that this is, for some of them, a very novel experience. Those six years of frustration while they were attempting to govern the country have suddenly burst forth; they have been relieved of responsibility. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, and all members of this house to bear with them in the great transformation which has come over them. We should not take all their remarks too seriously, because I am certain they are not meant too seriously. Surely the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) could not have meant all those things he said; and I am sure the little lecturer who spoke last night, the former parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance, did not mean them either. We enjoyed his lecture last evening. The philosophy he used must be this; do as I say, not as I do.
This was a bold budget and an imaginative one. As we have seen, it was obviously beyond the scope of certain members. All the things which this government advocates may not meet with the desired measure of success, but the fact remains that we have a government in Canada willing to take the action necessary to solve some of the chronic problems which have caused so much debate here. I am pleased that we have a government with the courage to act, with the
The Budget-Mr. Cashin imagination to cross new frontiers and with men and women capable of bringing these aims to fruition.
Certain hon. members of this house have amused me by their reactions to some of the things which have happened. I refer particularly to those hon. gentlemen sitting opposite me and to my right. It seems they have now become the new champions of strict adherence to custom, tradition and precedent. Evidently they do not approve of reaching for outside help. I must confess that I for one totally disagree with this most narrow view. I feel that far too often governments in their deliberations have been too cautious and too concerned about doing things in a particular way simply because this was the accepted way of doing things, the way which they had been done for years and years.
If progress is to be made by doing something differently, then we should do it. This generally is in keeping with good Liberal and good reform thinking. It would seem in light of their recent statements that hon. members opposite to my right have emerged as the new champions of the status quo. Fortunately for Canada, the populace decided they needed a new and vigorous government capable of adjusting the role of government to changing times and capable of using whatever brain power is needed in order to give the people who elected us their money's worth. I would like to think that the Canadian people have at long last a government which is not afraid to make departures from the ordinarily accepted way of doing things.
One of the most important departures we must make, it seems to me, is in the field of economic planning. This is a phrase which has been bandied about a great deal, and one which would seem to have different meanings to different hon. members. The former government felt that by setting up a number of sterile boards they had launched Canada on a great forward path. Their actions showed that not only were they unaware how to begin planning, but that they did not know what it was that needed to be planned.
There has always been a notion that private enterprise can function more efficiently than public enterprise and that consequently it is only in areas where private capital will not venture that it is respectable for public investment to operate. Yet we have seen, in the experience of other countries more rapidly developing than ours, the wisdom of energetic planning. I suggest that if we in this country are to make proper use of our natural resources, raise our national productivity, reduce unemployment and generally improve the living standards of the average

The Budget-Mr. Cashin Canadian, then our government must be prepared to venture forth with daring into hitherto unexplored areas.
I heard some hon. gentlemen opposite criticize the Minister of Finance for making statements in the budget address relative to matters three or four years hence. I do not criticize him for this; I praise him. Surely it would be a most backward step if the budget of a nation were brought down without long range proposals and if those responsible for its introduction regarded it in terms solely relative to the fiscal year in which it was introduced; that is to say, if they saw it as meaning merely an intention to raise so many dollars in a particular year and spend them in a certain way.
I suggest that in recent years the successive governments of our country have been too shortsighted. We must not only plan for our national development in terms of our present needs but we must be able to foresee as far as possible the consequences of our actions, and they must not be stop gap measures but part of an over-all plan. Some people feel that the change in the role of government since the thirties has gone too far. Others are content as long as no emergency arises. Still others point with pride to the fact that the welfare society in which we are supposed to be living has made great progress in the past 30 years as reflected in the lives of average Canadians. They would like to forget the fact that when one looks at the gap existing between people in low income groups and those in higher income groups, relatively little has changed.
I do not believe socialism is the answer. I think that with proper thought and study and by making available to our government and to parliament the best brains in this country and, indeed, in any other country, then and only then can we move forward at a faster rate. I think we have the means within our system to provide equal opportunities for all Canadians. While we have no doubt made progress, there is still a long road before us. I suggest that every young man or woman has a right to free educational opportunities at all levels, and that every family should be free from the torment of medical bills. I am not the first to advocate such things, but there is always the cry about the cost. The answer to that is, if this country is governed properly, and if we take the necessary measures to expand our economy, the money will be available. We shall not achieve it if we follow the narrow approach always taken by the hon. members in the Conservative party, an attitude which seems now to be expressed by our friends in the New Democratic party.

As hon. members are aware, I come front the newest province of the Dominion of Canada and, as a result, I am concerned about the treatment given by the government to primary producers in various fields. I suggest that up to now there has been unequal and unfair treatment. Yet if this country is to. develop and all Canadians given a fair chance, not only to make a living but to make a better living than that made by their forefathers, this government will have to adopt a broader view than that adopted by previous governments.
I refer particularly to the primary producers in the fishing industry. In the past they have not received attention commensurate with that received by agriculture. Mr. Speaker, Canada is the only important fish producing country in the world without a national fisheries development program. The individual fish producing provinces are obviously limited in what each of them can do. Fortunately we already have the assurance that a conference to discuss such a badly needed policy will be called shortly, and I think it is a significant omen for the success of this conference that the Prime Minister has already made an important announcement relative to the 12 mile limit which will, of course, be of considerable importance to the fishermen of this country. Mr. Speaker, this establishment of the 12 mile limit is just one of the steps to be taken by our government if anything constructive is to be done for our hitherto neglected fisheries. This does not answer the gnawing question of the great disparity in price between what primary producers and consumers have to pay.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are major obstacles created not by a lack of fish resources but which arise instead from the difficulties which are basic to primary industries. These are a deficiency in marketing development, in orderly marketing and price stability; inadequate insurance against yield uncertainty; the need for quality improvement; inadequacies in credit and in programs designed to help fishermen to adopt the latest in equipment and technology; and the need for development programs for communities attempting to adjust to changes in the fishing industry. If these problems are to be met at all they can only be solved within the context of a renewed program of national development.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in a house with such heavy representation from agricultural areas it may seem a little unusual to find speakers advocating the implementation of certain basic measures to reduce price uncertainty. However, at the present moment the fishermen of this country operate without a substantial degree of price assurance, yet

without this price assurance fishermen can-mot effectively plan their operations prior to the opening of the fishing season, nor can they plan or even afford a longer term investment program to raise their productivity.
Despite this need there is an amazing contrast, between price stability measures available to fishermen and those available to farmers. Between 1944 and 1962, when you adjust the difference in the number of people in agriculture and the number in fisheries, the fishermen received only one seventh of the price stabilization support given to farmers. The experience in agriculture suggests that price support for fishery producers can be substantially strengthened without [DOT]detriment to exports.
The comparison between agricultural and fisheries support programs does not end with stabilization measures. The gap in fisheries policy creates an urgent problem for fishermen concerned with salt fish products. The solution here, I suggest, would be the creation of a national marketing board similar to the Canadian wheat board, to provide fishermen with the price assurance and market organization they now lack. The deficiencies are far more appalling when we xealize that the number of fishermen, particularly in Newfoundland, is decreasing. Another of the major deterrents to a sound and planned investment by fishermen to increase their productivity is the risk of yield uncertainty. The availability of technical knowledge and improved equipment will reduce this risk. Nevertheless measures providing for some form of catch insurance or compensation are also needed.
In the field of agriculture, crop insurance since 1939 has cost the government $185 million, a sum 1,000 times greater than the federal costs under the fishermen's indemnity plan for loss of boats and gear; and no program exists to compensate fishermen for poor catch. I also might add that I believe in the vicinity of $123 million has been paid out in acreage payments to western farmers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not unaware of the differences between these two primary industries, but the great disparity between the government's concern for agriculture and its concern for fisheries must make it clear to all hon. members that the time has come to give equal treatment to our primary industries. In this regard I might mention that the Minister of Fisheries recently visited my province, and I can say made a tremendous impression there. I hope when this matter comes up for study it will have the support of all hon. members of this house, because I am sure it is in keeping with our thinking
The Budget-Mr. Cashin that if we can do this for one primary producer then surely primary producers in other fields are deserving of the same treatment.
In the earlier part of my remarks I commended this government as one which I believed would venture forth into-I believe these were the words I used-new and unexplored areas. Although I am not, and I do not think many hon. members here are, a financial or economic expert, when it comes to economics I am consoled somewhat when I look at the spectrum and see so many learned men in that field having such opposite views. I do not suppose that there is anything likely to cause so much disagreement. But I am inclined to support those who favour the concept of planning. This may, of course, mean that governments will get bigger; it will depend on how efficiently it is done.
Then on the other side of the coin we have people who in their overzealous regard for the freedom of the individual would drive our thinking back 20 or 30 years because they cannot comprehend this kind of government of which I am speaking operating in a society which permits the fullest freedom to the individual. I suggest that if there is a challenge to our time-there are, indeed, many-to me I see it as this; to be able to move forward in this new direction; to be able to have this more active participation by government yet at the same time preserve the freedom of the individual.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) introduced his famous budget which was prepared by outsiders, that is persons who had no mandate from the people to prepare such a budget.
As can be seen in the speech, the changes put forward in this budget do not favour the classes of society that built Canada and made it one of the most beautiful and one of the richest countries in the world as far as production is concerned.
In preparing this budget, the Toronto vested interests made sure that it was to their own advantage and to the prejudice of the worker and the farmer. But they overlooked an item which was detrimental to them. I refer to the 30 per cent tax on foreign investments in Canadian companies. And as soon as they realized their oversight, the present nightmare of the Minister of Finance began. The president of the Montreal stock exchange who is also the president of the Canadian stock exchange, Mr. Eric Kierans, the Liberals' great friend who campaigned against Social Credit in the April election, that socialist millionaire, as he liked to call himself during an interview with the press, that socialist and liberal millionaire who is interested in socializing everybody and everything except himself, soon came to the rescue of high finance, and that without the slightest embarrassment, in a jiffy, during an interview he had at 5.30 on June 18 with the Canadian Minister of Finance, he made the Minister of Finance change his mind and suspend the enactment of the 30 per cent tax on foreign investments

in Canada. And the Liberal party complied, obeyed, bowed and said: "Yes, boss", when faced with the demands of high finance to which it is much indebted since April 8 last.
Since the last general election, the Liberal party is more than ever forced to submit to high finance, to kowtow to it, to attend to its needs, to nurse it; and that, at the expense of the people, of the workers and of the farmers, because the election of the Liberal party and the campaigning against Social Credit in this country have been an expensive venture for the high finance.
The Liberal party committed a sin against high finance in its last budget, and the financiers soon called it to order, causing a turnabout, a political somersault, so that the bankers might go on abusing the people.
"Let us free the banking world from taxes and shift them upon the poor, upon those who have not the means to defend themselves," thought the Liberal party, because the more we shall free the financiers from taxation, the more they will be allowed to take advantage of the poor; the more poor people, the more rags; the more rags, the more paper; the more paper, the more dollars printed; the more dollars printed, the more capital created; the more capital created, the more cartels, trusts and banks that can be founded. The more banks you open, the more loans you promote with credit; the more loans, the more debts, and the more debts there are, the greater the number of poor people. And the poor are in rags and the vicious circle goes on with the old parties.
Those are the effects of a false, dishonest and crooked economic system which, in order to last brings about cycles which are called crisis, restriction and unemployment.
And to get out of unemployment in our economic context, we need war or a state of war or preparation for war or a national defence budget as the one we have this year.
Because with war you get destruction, and with destruction you get peace, and with peace re-employment comes back, and employment leads to prosperity, and prosperity leads to overproduction, and with overproduction there is unemployment, and unemployment leads to poverty and hunger, and when there is poverty and hunger people give up hope and wish for war, and that vicious circle goes on with the old parties and with an unrealistic financial system.
In this twentieth century, when we boast of the fact that we have harnessed water power, as well as all kinds of power, also that we have put water, air, machinery and atoms
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau at the service of man, and when billions of dollars are spent in the world to conquer space and visit other planets, after all those achievements by man, we have not even succeeded in taming money, in putting money at the service of production and production at the service of man.
Because money, Mr. Speaker, is only a means of exchange and we of the federal government continue to give free rein to a financial system which makes for the exploitation of man by man.
The indignation of Social Crediters at such a system has been going on for more than 30 years, Mr. Speaker. Our system leads to stagnation, depression, extreme poverty, while millions of potential consumers are still waiting for a minimum living wage.
During the last ten years, for instance, what did the two old parties do to escape the disastrous fate of a crisis of which there are already many signs? What did they do to permit a fair distribution of those goods which machinery is ready to produce in quantity and in quality?
Our financial system is like a youth who would have outgrown his child clothes and whose blood circulation would be affected by the pressure of his clothes on his arteries.
As soon as a war or some disaster rips his clothes, he comes to life again. When will we get rid of that financial strait-jacket which is choking our country? Surely, we will not do so by following the steps of the two old parties which believe that we can bring back prosperity to Canada by borrowing and imposing more taxes on Canadians.
In 1957, before the general election of March 31, the Conservatives gave the Canadian people the impression that if a Conservative government were elected, a big fight would be started against the Bank of Canada and the tight money policy of the Liberal party.
That comedy was a true repetition of the promises made by Mr. Mackenzie King in 1935 and which he consigned to oblivion once he was in power with a large majority.
Instead of fighting tight money, the Conservative party gave us a little more of all the things the Liberal party had been giving us before 1957.
And now that the Liberals are back in power they are preparing to give us a little more taxes than the Conservatives had given us after 1957.
The 1963 federal budget indicates that it will cost almost $1 billion in interest, merely

The Budget-Mr. Rondeau to finance our public debt. We see no trace of financial reform in the budget.
Taxes are boosted for the small wage earner, the worker, the farmer, the small industrialist. They are overburdened. They are investigated. They have to pay fines. That is all they are given: taxes and fines.
As a result of all those taxes, a smaller number of rich people will become richer and a larger number of poor will become poorer. Then some people will be surprised one day when the taxpayers rebel against the tax-gatherers.
Coming back to the budget, Mr. Speaker, I believe that it clearly indicates that it has not been prepared with an election in mind, because we know quite well that should that have been the case it would have probably been more advantageous for the people.
Family allowances would certainly have been increased, taxes reduced, no 11 per cent tax would have been imposed on building materials, a tax which affects the poor more than the rich.
It is claimed that unemployment will be reduced, but politicians pay only lip service to this objective, because with an 11 per cent tax on building materials, the only result will be an increase in the cost of construction, and, therefore, construction in Canada will decrease and unemployment will consequently increase and so will the price of houses, rents and the cost of living.
Taxes create unemployment, the unemployed require unemployment insurance and unemployment insurance requires increased taxes, this is the vicious circle of a ridiculous regime.
Having had the opportunity of sitting in this house when the Conservatives were in office in 1962, and having been re-elected to this twenty sixth parliament, I have been able to see to date what I believed for 20 years: both old line parties act exactly the same when in office.
They are the offspring of the same financial sire, and I am scandalized, Mr. Speaker, to see the negligence and the lack of seriousness of both old line parties when they consider the problems of a nation of close to 20 million.
They beat around the bush without ever finding a solution to the problem; they pretend to try and solve the problem, they launch surveys, they appoint boards, they

create new departments, they shift taxes, but they always make sure that they are raised at the same time.
And all the time, farmers and workers are living with the hope that a solution may be found, but they can be sure that they will never see the day when a solution is found and implemented.
To prove my remark to the effect that the people are sinking deeper into indebtedness, because of the inability on the part of the government to find a solution, I wish to quote a Canadian Press release published in La Presse of Montreal on June 7, 1963. That item was entitled:
Canadians' debts tripled since 1954.
-Canadians at the present time owe the banks, in personal unguaranteed loans, about three and a half times as much as they did in 1954.
Accounts in departmental stores, both current and revolving budget accounts, have doubled during the same period.
The dominion bureau of statistics estimates that the total outstanding amount of consumer's credit as at March 31 was $3,664,000,000, an increase of $301,000,000 in a year.
There are no figures available for unpaid accounts due doctors, dentists, hotels, transport companies and public services or concerning loans among individuals.
One of the most important increases which has taken place within one year relates to loans made by banks to individuals and payable at fixed dates. They have increased by 13 per cent, amounting to $1,206 million while the corresponding figure was $1,067 million on March 31, 1962. By the end of 1954, those loans amounted to $351 million.
While they amounted to $65 million on March 31, 1962, loans for home improvements made by the banks under the National Housing Act have only increased by 3.1 per cent in one year, to reach a total of $67 million.	___
Cash loans made by small loan companies went up from $572 million to $658 million within a year, an increase of 15 per cent.
Conditional sale agreements underwritten by loan companies for current consumer goods had reached a total of $771 million by the end of March, 1963, while the corresponding figure a year earlier stood at $732 million.
Accounts outstanding in department stores increased within a year from $324 million to $383 million. At the end of 1954, the corresponding figure was $186 million.
Three and a half times more debt than in 1954, that is to say a debt increase of 350 per cent, and that within eight years.
Why did the Canadian Press not mention that before the federal election, that is about two months before? If the aim of the Canadian Press is to guide the public and keep the people well informed, it would have been well-advised to publish that communique before the election, to put voters in a better position to judge both old line parties.
Three and a half times more debt than in 1954, and still the old line parties brag about prosperity. Who is crazy?

When the Conservatives were in power in 1962, they said everything was going fine under their regime, much better than under the Liberals.
They were defeated, and now they think everything is going wrong. As for the Liberals, when they were in opposition, they said everything was going wrong under the Conservatives, but now that they are in power, according to them, everything is going fine and people abroad have regained confidence in our economy.
When they are seated on your right, Mr. Speaker, the two old line parties both say everything is going fine, and when they find themselves on your left, both say things are going wrong. The only difference between your right and your left for the two old line parties, Mr. Speaker, is that the pork barrel is on your right, and it is then that things are going well. Bunch of jokers. The old line parties are the docile servants of financiers who pay for their elections and pay themselves back afterwards.
The Minister of Finance consults financiers to draw his budget in order not to displease them, and when he finds that part of it is not to their liking, he removes it to suit the wishes of the sharks of high finance, who have shown themselves in their true light at the last election and who now prove that only Social Crediters were right, because we were the only ones to denounce them.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) follows the dictates of the Americans with regard to nuclear arms because they gave so much to the election fund of the Liberal party to help them fight Social Credit, that they must now be paid back.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) sees the price of sugar rising to a scandalous height and that is also to pay back election expenses.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) penalizes the farmers for their plentiful milk production by cutting off the 25-cent subsidy per hundredweight as well as the lime subsidy. Everyone will pay many times over the election expenses of the Liberal party.
The budget of June 13 does not mention the farmers and the workers, except to increase their taxes.
Produce more, workers and farmers, and we will tax you more, because you are the two most productive social groups in the country? We must keep you poor, the two old line parties seem to say, because we want to be able to keep on exploiting you.
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
They can make pretty speeches, tell you that they will study your problem, that they are anxious to solve them, that you must be patient and they will help you, but these are only words and talk is cheap. And all this is rather easy. We will repeat those encouraging words at the next election and we will tell you again that farmers and workers are the cornerstone of our society. But after the election, we will put you a little deeper into debt, burden you with taxes and exploit you, as is the case since the last federal budget.
Our system is wrong, absurd and unhealthy, and it will lead us inevitably to ruin, because the Canadian parliament has surrendered its responsibilities in the most important field, that of money and credit.
Those who control money and credit have become our masters, to such an extent that "without their consent, one can no longer breathe", as stated by Pius XI in his encyclical Quadragesimo Anno.
The federal parliament reminds me somewhat of the owner of a car who would give it to his neighbour. When he needs it, he gives his neighbour 15 cents an hour to use his own car.
It is possible for the federal parliament, through the Bank of Canada, to obtain the credit it needs without borrowing this money or credit from private companies known as chartered banks.
Why pay 15 cents a mile to a neighbour in order to use one's own car? Why pay $1 billion in interests to chartered banks to supply our own credit, when we can do it ourselves through the Bank of Canada? It is just as stupid to pay $1 billion in interests to chartered banks than to pay 15 cents a mile to a neighbour for the use of one's own car.
Social Crediters are not against chartered banks as such. They are private institutions and it is only normal that they be authorized to lend their capital. But what we condemn, is that the federal government should allow chartered banks to create money under the form of credit and to lend it to individuals, provincial governments and school boards and, what is even more shocking, to lend that credit which is after all only figures, to lend those figures to the federal government, which should be the only one to have authority in that field.
The function of the banks is to lend money, not to create it. Now, when the

The Budget-Mr. Rondeau federal government gives the banks authority to open a credit account of $100 in favour of someone when all they have is $8 in available cash or in securities or in reserve funds, this means that the federal government gives the banks authority to lend $92 which they do not have. They can do it and as a matter of fact they do, by giving credit to the borrower who, after having signed an acknowledgement of indebtedness, can circulate $92 in cheques drawn on a new credit, which will be transferred from one bank account to another.
And the bank makes all those transactions without giving a single dollar and without even reducing the account of anybody.
Moreover, it will charge 6 or 6i per cent interest on 92 per cent of the money it lends, without having to disburse anything. That is creating money out of nothing, or creating credit money.
The creating of money is the responsibility of the supreme authority of a nation, which is the government. The issue of credit, which represents 92 per cent of all money today, should also be the responsibility of the federal government, which would control it through the Bank of Canada.
Why does the federal government borrow its money or its credit, when it can create it?
The bankers who had conferred upon them this power to create credit instead of the government, get such fabulous sums from this fraudulent transaction that, by means of their election funds, they easily control the politicians of the two old parties who could change those conditions if they were not bound hand and foot.
The politicians of the two old parties disagree as to colour, but they are the products of the same paint firm.
I would like to quote here some evidence submitted to the banking committee in 1954, by Frank O'Hearn, director of the office of valuation and exchange in Toronto, as printed in volume 2 of the minutes and evidence of the standing committee on banking and commerce.
Concluding a very long and interesting statement, he declared:
That on behalf of the 16 million Canadians who, without their knowledge, are deprived of $10 billion of savings in cash earned with great effort, and that to their greatest detriment.
And he added:


The chartered banks have at this time (in 1954) accumulated securities of all kinds, which amount to an approximate total of $10 billion. As strange as it may seem, they acquired all those assets from the Canadian people and the federal government, while paying absolutely nothing for it. What has come about because, first of all, banks have accumulated those holdings, without risking a single cent of their own money: they obtained everything by trickery. It is time for them to give back those ill-gotten gains or to pay for them.
Other statements along the same lines, and quite as interesting, have been made one after another, not by members of the Social Credit, but by people who could see through our stupid banking system. The difference between those people and ourselves, is that they saw what was wrong, as we see it, but they did not suggest any remedy, whereas we are advocating one.
It would only be a matter for the Bank of Canada of setting up an accounting system which would make it possible for Canadians to exchange their products between themselves. Because money, Mr. Speaker, is but a medium of exchange, simply a legalized measure of exchangeable values, work and wealth.
Money is a monetary measure just like other measures such as a cord of wood, a yard of cloth or a gallon of syrup. Wealth is the wood, the cloth or the syrup. The measures are the cord, the yard and the gallon.
Social Crediters would like to see the federal government through the Bank of Canada create as many measures as there are things to be measured in Canada, that is as much money as there is wealth.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to quote here a news report from the Canadian Press dated July 22, 1958 and published in a newspaper of southern Alberta, the Lethbridge Herald, which was founded and owned by the Liberal Senator Buchanan. This report was entitled: "Money, what it means", and I quote:
(Text):
To understand how borrowing money from the banking system can create money, it is necessary also to remember that money has more forms than currency and cents. While money exists in the form of currency, it also exists in the form of bank deposits, which are literally nothing more than entries in bank books. But they are transferred from one person's bank account to another's through the simple means of writing out cheques.
In the case of the last government's loan what the banking system did, in effect, was to create $400 million in bank deposits out of the air in exchange for the government's promise to pay back this amount in five months. Every time a bank makes a loan to anyone, new money is created in the same way. It's a kind of magic carried on with paper and bookkeeping entries.

(Translation):
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, you just have to look up the Bank Act, section 71, chapter 48, where it is clearly stated that:
The bank shall maintain a cash reserve in the form of a deposit with the Bank of Canada and of Bank of Canada notes held by the bank and such reserve shall be not less on the average during any month than eight per cent-
Consequently, for every $8 of money or values deposited with the Bank of Canada, chartered banks can lend $100.
In other words, they can grant credit at interest to anyone to the extent of $92. It is this power of the chartered banks to make credit which is not fully guaranteed, that the Social Credit party wants to take away from the banks to give it to the Bank of Canada which is the rightful property of the Canadian people.
The Bank of Canada would create credit for Canadians without borrowing or adding to the national debt; it would make social capital available for Canadians.
As evidence of the fact that the creation of credit by the chartered banks is highway robbery, you just have to refer to the combined annual reports of the eight chartered banks as of December 31, 1961. You will see that their net assets total $19 billion, whereas their paid-up capital is only $275 million.
By what feat have the banks succeeded in building up $19 billion of assets with only $275 million worth of paid-up capital. It is precisely this paid-up capital of $275 million that corresponds to the true liquid assets of the banks, nothing more. The rest is made up of whole cloth.
According to the Bank Act, chartered banks can lend up to 12| times the amount of their reserves or deposit liabilities, which means that for every dollar that they deposit with the Bank of Canada, they can lend $12.50 at 6J per cent which amounts to 81i per cent profits on the paid-up capital, not to mention the profits they make from management fees, exchange charges, etc. That is how they have been able to build up assets of $19 billion with a paid-up capital of $275 million.
Our financial structures would bring about any nations ruin. They will certainly lead us to bankruptcy, and stifle all our efforts, for they are geared towards a centralization of wealth, which necessarily results in the exploitation of man by man.
Why does the federal government not use its own bank, the Bank of Canada, for the necessary financing, instead of looking for loans, sinking deeper into debt, and increasing the taxation burden to pay the interests 28902-5-92i
The Budget-Mr. Scott
on that debt? The federal government could easily ask the Bank of Canada to finance its various transactions.
The government could use the Bank of Canada like a man at the wheel, and through careful steering, keep a straight enough course.
By wisely directing the bank along the right financial road, the government could lead this country's economy into the proper channels, do away with debts and interests on debts, and clear up the confusion brought about by our topsy-turvy financial system.
When on June 18 the president of the Montreal stock exchange addressed himself in such a threatening fashion to the Minister of Finance, and in view of the fact that foreign investors wanted to withdraw from Canada because of the 30 per cent capital levy on foreign investments in this country, why did the Minister of Finance not reply: Well, in that case we shall use Canadian funds, through the Bank of Canada. We shall thus allow Canadian shareholders to buy shares back from you, and we intend to manage our own resources with our own credit.
As for capital-
