speechtext:
On rising to participate in the budget debate let me say I do not wish to spend any time on the circumstances surrounding the drawing up of the budget and its presentation. I think too much time has been spent on that already. It is more important, in my opinion, to try to analyse the budget itself rather than the circumstances surrounding it. I do not want anything to distract from an examination of some of the aspects of this budget. While attempting to do so it is not my desire to urge upon the government any of our philosophical beliefs which it may not be able to accept. This budget, like all budgets, is part good and part bad. There are some good measures in it and we should be unfair if we did not admit it immediately. I do not want to mention them. Indeed, there is no necessity for me to do so since government speakers are notoriously not reluctant to publicize their own virtues.
There are three aspects of the budget that I should like to examine particularly. The first is the attempt to increase employment and stimulate the housing and construction industries. The second aspect I should like to analyse is the attempt to deal with the problem presented by foreign control of our

The Budget-Mr. Scott economy and the degree to which countermeasures are likely to be successful. The third matter I should like to consider might be called an omission from the budget. How is this budget going to help Canada get into the trading blocs which are forming in the world? To what degree do these proposals support the work of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp)?
In discussing the budget in relation to the housing and construction industry it becomes clear that the intention of the government is to stimulate this section of the economy. The proposals put forward by the Minister of Finance seek to do this in two ways. First, a sales tax of 11 per cent is imposed on building material acquired in Canada. This is expected to produce revenue of some $370 million. First of all, let me say it is widely accepted that a sales tax is the most regressive type of taxation possible. . It affects all wage earners in Canada to the same extent, regardless of their actual income. The imposition of such a tax has already had a catastrophic effect on the construction industry. Yesterday, the halls of the House of Commons were flooded with people who had come from all over Canada to protest the imposition of this tax and to outline to hon. members and, presumably, to hon. members in the government, and those who support the government, the serious effect this tax will have on the construction industry. A roar of opposition is coming from coast to coast. In my own constituency, one of the largest manufacturers of furnaces and air conditioners has given everybody in his plant a week's notice and told them all he does not intend to carry on. He says this tax is the last straw and that costs have now become prohibitive. Well, that is an excellent way of expanding the economy.
The second thing the government is attempting to do in the field of the construction industry and housing is to change the National Housing Act regulations around. For these efforts, the government honestly deserves the booby prize. It is almost impossible to understand how they could have brought down such a proposal. They hope, by changing these regulations, to have more homes built and to reduce the amount of the down payment. I suggest that neither of these aims will be achieved. First, the government brings in a measure to give a bonus of $500 to anyone who buys a new house built during the wintertime. All the construction experts tell us that the extra cost of building a house in the wintertime is $600. This will be added to the end price of the house, so the first attempt to stimulate building will have no

practical effect because the price of the house will increase by more than the amount of the bonus.
The second provision is a reduction by one quarter per cent in the interest rate paid under the N.H.A. mortgage. Well, if that is amortized over the life of the mortgage it will save the purchaser approximately $450. The 11 per cent tax on building materials will increase the price of a house by $600. Thus, the two measures presented to us as a stimulant to the housing industry will be totally ineffective. As I said earlier, it is hard to understand why a government would bring in such a provision. I would be interested to know if it was ever discussed with anybody in the construction industry or with anybody in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I ask this because, to my mind, the proposal is completely impracticable. I predict with complete confidence that it will have the opposite effect to the one which was intended. It will lead to higher prices, higher mortgages, larger carrying charges and increased down payments. For one thing, the granting of a $500 bonus in respect of houses built during the winter is already discouraging people from having houses built in the summertime. People are waiting in order to get the grant. What this demonstrates is a lack of knowledge on the part of the government with regard to the housing industry, the same absence of knowledge that it showed in another field when it sought to bring in a 30 per cent tax on share transfers of Canadian companies.
We are really missing the boat in housing. If we examine income tax returns in Canada, we find that in 1961 there were 2,500,000 people in Canada who were earning less than $4,000 a year. In that same year, the number of people earning less than $4,000 a year who were able to buy homes under the National Housing Act was 2,293. So the provision made in the budget is directly contrary to the trend we should be trying to encourage in housing today, that is to say, lower prices and lower interest rates so that a larger number of Canadian wage earners can buy their own homes.
In summary, it is hard to understand why a government which claims to be really interested in an expansion of the construction industry would single out for the lash of new taxation the one sensitive industry in the country which has the greatest potential for providing employment. Why would the government take this particular industry and handicap it and cripple it in the way these two proposals must do? I hope that at some stage an explanation will be forthcoming

from the minister, and that he will tell us the reason for this surprising step.
The other aspect of our aifairs with which I should like to deal for a moment is the section of the budget which purports to deal with the problem of foreign ownership. The aim expressed in the budget is an admirable one, namely, that we in Canada must at some stage regain control of our own economy. This question has been discussed in the house many times. It is well known there is no other country in the world whose resources are controlled in so large a part by residents outside its shores. In the beginning, the need for foreign capital was a very real one. However, in the course of time extensive difficulties have been created as a result of the entry of foreign capital in such large amounts. We know that important decisions by many companies in Canada are made outside our borders. We know that decisions affecting exports by Canadian companies are made by parent companies elsewhere, and this complicates our whole export program. We need a decision as to expansion and relocation, and the hiring and firing of our men south of the border under other companies' control. We know that the outflow of dividends is creating financial strains on our economy. If the dividends are not paid to companies in the United States they are reinvested in Canada to buy up more of our country and accentuate the problem.
What has the government proposed in this regard? There seems to me to be two objectives. First of all the government told us that its long run objective on this important subject is for us to acquire 25 per cent interest in foreign controlled companies. It is hard to understand the reason for this 25 per cent. The minister in his speech said that this will provide a voice for the Canadian people. It will also provide a point of view, but it will provide absolutely no control whatsoever. It is hard to understand why the government says 25 per cent interest is a long run objective. What has really happened is that the "six buck boys" have turned into 25 per cent Canadians. The objective of a 25 per cent interest is not good enough if we are serious about meeting this problem over the long run.
The methods the government has proposed are twofold. First of all they propose this 30 per cent tax on the transfer of shares. This lasted for about four days, has now disappeared in a roar of opposition from stock exchanges both here and in the United States, and probably will not appear again. Its disappearance is highly significant, because what
The Budget-Mr. Scott it points out is that the degree of foreign ownership of the Canadian economy has become so strong and extensive and powerful that this type of attempt to deal with the problem is doomed to failure. The exterior influences which can be exerted on our economy are so strong that this type of limited measure simply will not work. That to me is the real significance of the attempt to impose this tax, even though it was unsuccessful.
The second method adopted has been the attempt to fluctuate the withholding tax depending on whether or not the company has a 25 per cent Canadian owned content in it. This again will undoubtedly turn out to be just as unworkable and impracticable as the other scheme. A day or two ago a New York investment company did a survey of what it would cost to acquire a 25 per cent interest in 37 of the major companies which are now foreign owned. It was estimated that it would take a minimum of $4 billion and that the share capital required if unloaded on the market would demoralize and paralyse every stock exchange in Canada. So that of the two methods being used by this government to cure the problem of foreign ownership, I suggest one is already out of the window and the other will prove to be impracticable and unworkable.
The reason for this is because you cannot deal with the problem of foreign control over the economy by assessing penalties and imposing restraints upon foreign investors. The solution to a problem of this magnitude lies, I suggest, right here in Canada, because first of all we have to begin to generate as much of our own developed capital as we can within our borders. Second, we have to convince Canadians that Canada is worth investing in and have to urge them more and more to put their savings into their own country. So that the solution to foreign ownership does not lie in imposing bludgeoning penalties against investors.
In trying to deal with the problem we must accept the idea that foreign investment is still needed, and will continue to be needed for some time. We cannot take some action which is going to restrain this and suddenly cut it off. We can only do that after we have generated our own capital. But if we are to borrow abroad to develop our Canadian companies let the government do it by way of floating loans in the United States or elsewhere, bring the money to Canada, and through the Canadian development fund lend the money to our businessmen here. Then let the businesses use those funds to expand their growth, and when they pay the money back to the government the government can pay it back to the exterior force from which they

The Budget-Mr. Scott borrowed it. In this way the expansion is kept within our own borders and we can avoid this continual alienation of our own resources. We in this group hope that the development fund which the government has proposed will turn out to be something with teeth in it to provide the capital we need to expand our economy.
We should also interest our trust and loan companies in the business of lending and get the government itself to invest in our own resource industries. That is another aspect which has received too little attention here. If at some date all the methods of stimulation of capital in this country fail and it is necessary in the long run to reacquire control of some of these industries, we still have available to us the technique of public ownership where these industries which have been alienated abroad can be made responsible to the Canadian people once again. It seems to me that somewhere along this line lies the solution to the biggest single problem facing Canada today, namely foreign control. You cannot meet the problem by this kind of discriminatory taxation. All you are doing is helping the Canadian capitalist at the expense of the United States capitalist and it will not work. We have had the example where already the first proposal made by the government has been rescinded and the second is just as impracticable. In short, the government has set out on the road and they are just playing with the problem in restricting themselves to these sorts of measures.
Another matter is the lack in the budget of any type of financial help for the building of hospitals. I know we have been told by the government that we have to wait four or five years for the medicare plan, and we will have to accept that. But in the interval surely something could be done to deal with the scandalous hospital shortage in this country. In the area of Scarborough, which is part of my riding, we have 99,000 children under the age of 15 years. We have exactly 22 children's hospital beds to accommodate them. We have no isolation beds, beds for mentally disturbed children, for chronically ill children or for adolescents. The hospital shortage is reproduced, I am sure, from coast to coast and is a scandal which should be looked into. I do not understand why the government is not prepared to increase the grants which it is making for the construction of hospitals. The municipalities simply cannot afford to do it, and the biggest joke of all is that one of the institutions exempt from assistance under the municipal loan board is a hospital.
The last aspect of the budget upon which I wish to comment concerns the problem of trade. A great deal has been said in the house about the need to expand our export markets,
[Mr. Scott.l
to participate in the Kennedy round of trade proposals, and for Canada to make the fullest possible contribution in this regard. One thing which is missing in the budget, among many others, is a declaration of a fiscal and monetary policy for world trade. I have reviewed the budget and can see nowhere any indication that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) intends to give financial and fiscal support to the proposals of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). Without those proposals, and that backing, all of the minister's efforts to expand trade and to participate in trade negotiations will be wasted and useless.
What we really need in Canada, and need desparately, is a trade adjustment act of our own. This would enable negotiators to be sent to trade conferences to bargain for tariff concessions, which are going to have a troublesome effect in the short run on our economy.
We must have a trade adjustment act in this country so that our negotiators will know, if they make any concessions that are going to hurt our industries over a short time, the government is prepared to back up those decisions with regard to trade by assistance to industry, and by assistance to help workers move from place to place during the transition stage. But there is not a single thing in the budget which indicates that the government is prepared to do this.
The real tragedy of it all is that time is running out for Canada. Anyone at all conversant in any way with trade problems realizes that the negotiations which will take place over the next year or two will have a highly vital bearing on our future, and our negotiators must go into them armed with all weapons possible. I am suggesting that the absence of a trade adjustment act and any real monetary and fiscal policy to back up the Minister of Trade and Commerce will result in all this activity proving fruitless and unsuccessful.
Those are the three aspects of the budget on which I want to comment, and in closing I just want to say what I said at the beginning. There are good measures in the budget, but in at least three fields the government has failed very badly. In the field of housing it simply does not understand how the house market works, and if the government would only talk to its backbenchers, a lot of whom are conversant with it, it would realize the difficulties that will arise.
In the field of foreign ownership the government is just playing around the subject because the measures it has introduced simply cannot and will not be effective. Finally, in the field of trade relations we must at some stage have a strong, firm policy, with monetary and fiscal backing, when we enter trade

negotiations. In these three fields the government has failed in the budget now before us.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in presenting his budget the Minister of Finance remarked, as is recorded at page 996 of Hansard for June 13:
-it is my further duty to indicate the kind of measures which are needed to put our national affairs in order once again.
This then will be a "face the facts" budget.
Since then developments have proved that the Minister of Finance was quick to realize that the so-called facts are very hard to face, especially by himself.
During the election campaign the Liberal party cried much about the need for stable government. I am reminded of the remark made by the leader of the New Democratic party about a stable government. I must agree with his reference-the smell is definitely with us. Outside experts were brought in to work on the budget, and the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) who spoke earlier this afternoon, referred to the fact that the previous government had difficulty in getting experts to come to Ottawa. Does he not realize that our government departments are filled with experts for the express purpose of looking after the affairs of the country, and particularly so in the forming of a budget? If he had in mind outside experts then all I can say with reference to the fact that we failed to get them is: weren't we lucky?
With regard to the use of outside experts, in terms more familiar to me and the people of my constituency, it is quite evident that the Liberal party supports the use of moonlighters, because any man who is employed by a company, who receives pay from that company and then makes himself available for other work is nothing less than a moonlighter. It surprises me that my colleague from Cape Breton, the Minister of Labour, did not in some way point out to the Minister of Finance what a serious mistake this was.
These moonlighters are creating a serious situation within the civil service. Their employment could involve job security, and there is no doubt that it will be detrimental to future administration. There is every reason to believe that the pride of our senior civil servants has been injured, and I believe that in a lot of cases they are staying on only because of their dedication to the country in spite of the fact that they bypass jobs in outside industry which hold more potential and greater advantage for them.
I should like to refer for a moment to a report in this morning's Montreal Gazette which reads as follows:
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
Prime Minister Pearson came to Mr. Gordon's defence Thursday by saying after a cabinet meeting that there is no question of Mr. Gordon's resignation.
There is only one interpretation to be taken from that statement, and it is that the matter of the resignation of the Minister of Finance was discussed by the cabinet. We appreciate the fact that the cabinet only discusses very serious matters and, if the matter was so serious as to be discussed in the cabinet, why should it not be passed over to a special parliamentary committee to be examined further? The government is reversing the trend. Usually matters go forward from parliamentary committees to the cabinet level, but that is being reversed in this instance. I can only hope the government will let a committee have an opportunity to go into the very serious violations of budget secrecy that have taken place in the last few days.
The Liberals talk about indecision. There was certainly enough indecision during the last two days. As yet we are not aware whether there has been a suspension or withdrawal of the 30 per cent take-over tax. It surprises me that Liberal backbenchers have not spoken about this because I am sure they have received representations from industries in their own constituencies about the effect of it.
They also have not mentioned the 11 per cent tax on building materials, and in replying to the hon. member for Vancouver East, who stated that 5,000 workers were to be laid off in Vancouver as a result of that tax, the minister had the audacity and arrogance to give a flat no when asked to reconsider it. One can only contrast that attitude with the attitude he must have adopted to the committee led by Liberal Senator Gelinas, which met with him very recently. The minister backed down at the request of that committee, and I cannot understand the arrogance of a government refusing to listen to the representations of hon. members in opposition, in fact, I am quite sure government backbenchers share some of our views on this matter.
It is interesting to recall the attack made on the pegged dollar by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) last year. I am sorry the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is not in his seat as there are a few things I would like to call to his memory, but there is no reference to altering the pegged Canadian dollar in the budget. One remark made about the pegged dollar by the Minister of Finance was to the effect that he was the first person to state publicly that

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis devaluation caused a stagnation of the economy. That is a quotation from the Minister of Finance who attacked the pegging of the Canadian dollar and yet he has left the situation unchanged in the budget.
No doubt the detrimental effects of the budget are being brought to the attention of every hon. member of the house, including the backbenchers of the Liberal party and some members of the cabinet. I have here a letter received today from Nova Scotia and for the benefit of hon. members I should like to bring to their attention the results of the budget in my own province. It reads as follows:
We are enclosing a letter.. . that expresses our feelings exactly regarding sales tax on building supplies, especially lumber. Complying with government regulations makes so much extra work and expense, combined with 11 per cent increase in price to our customers, which has made a major decrease in our volume, has caused us to close down part of our manufacturing business, which means five men unemployed. This factory has run continuously for approximately 50 years but cannot struggle along any longer under these conditions.
The economy. . . has been struck hard, for we have been advised of quite a number of cancellations already by people who planned to put up new buildings, and many workers are being laid off at what should be the peak of the construction season. We are bringing this to your attention so that you will know in which direction the 60 day economy is rolling.
And further, in another letter:
The application of the federal sales tax to lumber is practically without precedent, and there will be many unforeseen developments throughout our industry, as well as allied industries. In the writer's opinion this is the greatest backward step taken by any government in so far as this industry is concerned in the last 50 years. We hope that all associations connected with the building trades will voice their disapproval of this matter through the proper channels in Ottawa.
The disapproval voiced by many opposition members is naturally falling on the very deaf ears of the Minister of Finance. It appears that the minister only has an ear for delegations led by senators recently appointed by the Liberal party.
I should like for a few moments to make some remarks about the Atlantic development board. I have not had too much to say on this matter so far. In my view the information given to us recently by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) was most welcome, and I refer to the fact that the $100 million made available for the Atlantic development board has turned out to be a floor and not a ceiling, to use his exact words. It is my hope that everybody throughout the Atlantic provinces will take notice of this statement and, rather than allowing the committee to be set up to report back to the government, will make known to everybody in their own localities what their hopes, plans and projects are so

that we who have the responsibility can watch very closely with the hope that any project will get the rightful consideration due it and that this will in some way or other prove beneficial.
I might also refer to something else that is very favourable so far as the Atlantic development board is concerned and I trust that the government will follow through on it. I have in mind the fact that there are six more appointments to be made to that board and it will be very interesting to see from what fields they will come. I trust the government will follow through and I will be only too happy to see what their intentions are in this matter. I am not concerned about the party or political background of these people. The fact is that if they come from these particular categories it will be most welcome. I do not know whether the Prime Minister realizes it but he stated in Fredericton, New Brunswick, that the personnel of the board should be expanded to include representation from labour, from fishing, from mining, from agriculture and from lumbering. That leaves just one appointment over and above these five categories. It will be very interesting to see if he follows through on his commitment to appoint a representative of labour, a fisherman, a mining man, a man from agriculture and somebody from lumbering. If this is brought about I am quite sure that the Atlantic provinces will have representation across the board and we will look for very active participation inasmuch as they will have come from fields such as labour, fishing, mining and so on.
The problem of spending $100 million should not be a difficult one. It is not too long ago that there was a provincial election in Newfoundland brought about by the idea that something had to be done for the fisheries, and the fact that Mr. Smallwood wanted $70 million for the fishing industry. After Mr. Smallwood was successful in the election he wasted no time in coming to Ottawa to the previous government to look for the $70 million. Let us hope that the present government, with which he is very closely associated through the Secretary of State, will see that Mr. Smallwood gets his $70 million for the fisheries. I look at it this way, Mr. Speaker, that if it is good for Newfoundland it is good for the maritime provinces generally and if it is good for the Atlantic provinces it is good for Canada. If the present government can get away from the arrogant attitude they have recently adopted and realize that fact Mr. Smallwood should get his $70 million before too long.
While I am on the subject of Newfoundland may I say that, while I have not heard anything, I imagine representations are being

made by Newfoundland and especially by the Secretary of State to restore term 29 of the terms of confederation which was a bone of contention for some time in that province.
The three year incentive to industries in slower moving though not depressed areas is a welcome one, but I would remind the Minister of Finance, being the brain or expert that he is-I will have something to say about that later too-that he must realize that no company of any consequence will look only three years ahead. Any company of any consequence establishing anywhere is going to look far beyond three years and in all probability will not look for a taxable profit in the first three years in any case. Any company establishing in any area on the basis of this inducement only will not and cannot contribute too much to the economy of any slow moving area.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
I might say that along with the legislation passed by the previous government the crown owned, independently operated Industrial Estates Limited in Nova Scotia has made tremendous strides in that province and in this calendar year alone 10 or 11 new industries have been established.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs made some kind of interjection. He did not quite get it across but if Hansard got it possibly I will have an opportunity to raise a question of privilege. The Secretary of State this afternoon figured that he had a question of privilege with regard to something that happened a few days ago, but I think there was a precedent established yesterday that there was a time limit of 15 minutes so far as raising questions of privilege is concerned. One of our members raised a question of privilege and he was told that 15 minutes had passed during which he had the opportunity to bring it forward. So, keeping in mind a possible question of privilege, I will follow the example set by the Secretary of State and not the example that was forced upon my colleagues in the house.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue my remarks about the arrogance of this party which has been carried forward from previous years. An example of this arrogance is the attitude towards the house taken by the Minister of Finance. There is plenty of it, I am told about $12 million worth. This is the same minister who, not too long ago during a television broadcast told the nation that the Liberal party had the platform and, "we think we have the leader." In this case, I think he shares a problem with the Secretary of State for External Affairs as the only members in 28902-5-93
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis the house who recognize that the prime minister sits across the floor and the leader sits on their side.
Again, I should like to cite the Secretary of State as a prime example of the arrogance, not only that the members of the official opposition have had to bear, but which has been extended to the members of his own party. Someone in our party referred to him as the actual leader of the party, and he may be right. I refer to him as the guardian angel, and if you do not believe me I refer you to what the Secretary of State said. This arrogance is applied not only to the members of the opposition, but it is applied to the members of the Liberal party. In this connection, I would just reread this passage of Hansard so that hon. members would fully understand what one of the ministers had to say about his own members. I quote from page 1267 of Hansard:

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Judging from the applause, Mr. Chairman, with which my entry was greeted, I take it that my little strategem worked and that hon. members opposite thought when I went out that I had left the building and the government would be caught napping.
Well, if that is not arrogance, I do not know what is and it is applied not only to the opposition. There is arrogance applied to the members of the Liberal party. He is saying that the only hope you have of not getting caught napping is for the Secretary of State to be present in the house or for somebody on this side to make sure you are kept awake.
Dealing further with this question of arrogance, I should like to cite the attitude of the government towards the setting up of the special defence committee. The Prime Minister stated at the time the committee would look into all aspects of defence. A question was raised as to whether or not there would be an opportunity of inquiring into previous commitments. The Secretary of State for External Affairs informed the house that this would not be possible because of security problems. Here is a conflict. The Prime Minister tells us we will look into all aspects and the Secretary of State for External Affairs says we cannot because of security problems. I do not believe it is the fault of the members of the opposition that there is such a thing as a security risk in this instance. If there is a security risk at all it is because of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer).
Why do I say this? I say this because of the minister's own statement in this house not too long ago. This is another indication of the arrogance of this party. Here is what the present Minister of National Defence

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis had to say in the House of Commons on February 4, 1963, as recorded on page 3426 of Hansard:
We were briefed by Admiral Smeeton, deputy commander of the Atlantic fleet, by General Calmel, deputy chief of staff of supreme allied headquarters ... A number of questions have been asked as to what our commitments to NATO are. I realize that this information is presumably classified, but I could never understand why it was, so I am going to take the responsibility tonight of saying what they are.
He realized this information was classified. It could be, therefore, that the security risk in this house is our present Minister of National Defence and perhaps the allied chiefs of staff realize this. Furthermore, if there is a possibility of a breach of security relating to commitments of this former government, why is it that the Liberal candidates have so much to say about previous commitments? If, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs says, this question cannot be opened up because of security risks, why is it the Liberal candidates have had so much to say on this question? Have they been made aware of what these so-called commitments are? On what authority have they been stating that there are commitments? This house is still seeking that information. I think it would be the responsibility of the defence department to indicate exactly what the government intends in this particular committee.

The dazzled Conservatives and Social Crediters dare ask the question: "What have you done about the 60 days of decision?" It will be a great pleasure to answer that question but before, I should like to recall very briefly the main events during the years of Conservative administration and what my friends opposite have done during those five years of indecision. On two occasions-

Twice, their minister of finance refused to submit a budget to parliament and to the Canadian people.
During five years, the deficits piled up, year after year, and yet the government did nothing to solve any of the important problems which existed. In five years, our friends opposite managed to accumulate a deficit exceeding $3 billion.

speechtext:
I feel that the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) is not qualified to teach anyone anything about budgetary administration.
During five years, unemployment remained at a level comparable to the one that existed during those Conservative years between 1930 and 1935, under the leadership of Mr. Bennett.
For five years, Canada saw its prestige deteriorating abroad; its relations with our friends to the south, the Americans, became very strained.
For five years, the value of the Canadian dollar kept on going down. In five years, those people who are accusing us, managed to drain the unemployment insurance fund in which we had left $1 billion, accumulated during the years we were in office.
28902-5-93J
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
For five years, the prime minister of the Conservative government avoided the numerous problems which were piling up before his eyes, instead of trying to solve them. He behaved like an ostrich before a stranger, which buries its head in the sand and thinks it is safe although its rear end is sticking out.
In five years, the members of the Conservative cabinet showed total confusion and a pitiful lack of solidarity which resulted in the resignation of several members of the Diefenbaker cabinet: confusion at national defence headquarters, confusion in the famous Coyne case, confusion with regard to unemployment, pitiful confusion with regard to the Columbia river, confusion, indecision, insecurity, deficits, waste, that is what we got from five years of Conservative rule from 1958 to 1963. And then, on April 8, 1963, on election day, the people of Canada gave to the Liberals and to the present Prime Minister a clear mandate to restore some order in the affairs of the country which had been neglected for five years.
The Prime Minister lost no time in getting to work. He announced that parliament would meet for a regular session as early as the middle of May. He superseded Conservative indecision by a Liberal program of 60 days of decision.
During those 60 days of decision, the Liberal government drew up a long list for anyone to see, a long list of important proposals designed to straighten out the affairs of the country. It will now be up to our friends opposite to help us pass the legislation required for the enactment of those measures that are essential to the future of our country.
Among government's decisions, let us mention the following: proposed royal commission on biculturalism, setting up of a standing committee of the house on national defence, creation of a department of agriculture for the east, establishment of a department of industry, setting up of a Canadian economic council, federal aid to municipal work in order to fight unemployment through the creation of loan funds for municipalities, and numerous other important measures with the sole purpose of stemming the economic depression resulting from five years of Conservative administration.
Mr. Speaker, the present Prime Minister of Canada is known all over the world as a man of decision; the energy he has shown in the last two months has won him the admiration of all the Canadian people. While our eminent Prime Minister works to rebuild

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis the finances and business of this country and the Minister of Finance introduces a budget filled with worth-while measures, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker)-who is now entering the house-and the remainder of his famous team of 210 members in 1958, are engaged in the worst kind of witch-hunt.
Thus, just a few days ago, namely on June 17 last, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition stood up and proposed with a quaver in his voice the adjournment of the house. Why? Here is what he said, as recorded on page 1235 of Hansard:
-adjourned to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the admission by the Minister of Finance on Friday, June 14 of facts relating to the preparation of the budget, which facts constitute a flagrant departure from constitutional budgetary practice, imperil-
That is according to the Leader of the Opposition.
-the traditional and essential secrecy of the budget, and which have had an unsettling effect on this house and on the country.
And even if he was very vehement in making that charge the Leader of the Opposition took good care not to substantiate it. He wanted to put on a big act. So, putting out his chest to impress people opposite in the galleries and again taking the tone he was using in the good old days of 1957, the Leader of the Opposition, eyes left and then right, made charges. He wanted to throw the facts at his audience. He made charges and, in the name of British tradition which is so dear to him and which he felt was threatened by the present Minister of Finance, he pointed his finger and made charges.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) offered to launch immediately the budget debate. And what did the Leader of the Opposition do? He refused his offer. The great man refused. He fulminated, he protested, he rebelled.
And what prompted that big act?
Just think that the Minister of Finance consulted people who did not belong to the federal civil service. What a terrible think to do. In so doing has the Minister of Finance violated a law? We asked the members of the opposition that question and they answered that he did not violate any law.
Has the secrecy of the traditional budget speech been violated? Was the secret known before the minister made his speech? Not at all. Had the three persons involved been sworn in as required by law? Are they loyal subjects of Her Majesty? Yes.
Therefore, if the Minister of Finance did not take any illegal action, if secrecy was


not violated, in short if he has not broken any law, what are the Leader of the Opposition and the members of the N.D.P. complaining about?
It has been said that by consulting advisers who were not federal civil servants, he violated the hallowed tradition or the darn tradition.
And that is all. That is the crime, that is the tragedy. The Minister of Finance violated a tradition which was so dear to the heart of the hon. member for Prince Albert, the former prime minister and the present Leader of the Opposition for some time yet.
The people of Canada will not be misled by tactics of hon. members opposite. The Canadian people understand that we finally have a Minister of Finance who can take advice. It pleases them to see that the present incumbent does not think he knows it all as his predecessor did for several years. The hon. member for Davenport does not think he is another Macdonald, another Napoleon Bonaparte or even another Donald Fleming.
The present Minister of Finance has just done what our friends in the opposition should have done during five years. He sought advice from competent people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Can you prove that they are competent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Naturally, if the minister had sought the counsel of the member for Edmonton West, the former speaker of the house, I would have told him that he was making a mistake, but he consulted competent people.
We finally have a Minister of Finance who does not take himself for Don Quixote nor for Mr. Gilles Gregoire. He admits that he might need advice, that he can be mistaken and that he can change his mind on occasion as he did this week. He proved it and we are glad to see that the Minister of Finance can change his mind. That is how the Liberal party remained in power for 22 years; it was flexible enough to change its mind when necessary.
What a contrast, Mr. Speaker, with the present Leader of the Opposition who, when he was the head of the government, thought that he could teach a thing or two to Mr. Coyne in economics. He also thought that he knew better than the minister of national defence did in his own field, that he knew better than everybody else and would accept advice from no one, not even from his best ministers like George Hees, Davie Fulton and others.

Those are facts. Where is the Leader of the Opposition today? He is in the opposition party pending a congress of the Conservative party.
If consultation of Canadian citizens is contrary to the Conservative tradition, well, the present Minister of Finance has put an end to such a sad tradition which has turned the traditional Tory party into a party of bad administrators, a party which has always governed badly each time it has had the opportunity to work out the destiny of this country since confederation.
As I was saying, for the Minister of Finance to take the advice of experts outside the federal civil service, was no violation of any law. And our friends opposite have not proven at all that the minister transgressed any law whatsoever. He assured himself that the secrecy concerning the preparation of the budget would be safely guarded until the very last minute when it was presented in the Commons. Nobody can prove that the secrecy was betrayed.
The Minister of Finance had those three advisors sworn in, as required by law. He did nothing, absolutely nothing which was illegal. I would rather say that he behaved very well.
We shall leave the Conservatives to carry on their witch-hunt. We shall leave the Leader of the Opposition carry on his performance and as for us on this side of the house we shall keep on working in the best interests of our country, Canada.
The future will tell that the brilliant member for Davenport was right. History will recognize the Liberals of today as men of decision, as truly efficient administrators.
We do not pretend to accomplish miracles. We do not propose to remove all taxes, to print money as some of our friends would. If we are not now as happy as we would like to be, it is just because we had to endorse for a few weeks the actions of our friends opposite. We had of course to endorse, in order to administer the country for a few months, the decisions taken by our hapless predecessors.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, that the situation will change very rapidly in our country.
Before concluding, I should like to deal briefly with a matter that is making the headlines at the present time; the future of Canadian federalism.
I was listening last evening to the very congenial and gentle member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) who gave us in this house a circus performance worthy of his master, the Leader of the Opposition.
My great friend from Brome-Missisquoi was worrying too, in a quavering voice, about
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis what the Liberals were going to do for national unity and for biculturalism. It is strange that nothing of the kind, not even the refusal of his leader to establish a commission on biculturalism, seemed to worry him last year when he was sitting on the government side.
I wish to reassure him and all our hon. friends; with the present Prime Minister, we can look to the future with confidence as far as national unity is concerned. It is worth while reminding the house and the country that the present Prime Minister was the first English speaking political leader to request an investigation on biculturalism in Canada. We commend him for it and we appreciate his courage and sense of dignity.
Hon. members opposite know that the present Prime Minister will set up shortly a royal commission of inquiry in that respect.
I should also like to remind the house that our leader has promised to provide Canada with a distinctive national flag and to recognize "O Canada" as the official national anthem within two years after the Liberal take-over.
That is what we call a government of action, and a Prime Minister of decision.
We will have our flag and our national anthem. We will have our inquiry on biculturalism. We will have our federal-provincial conference which will enable us to renegotiate the details of the confederative pact. We will hold a dialogue with the provinces. We will make Canada over. Wb believe in the unity and greatness of our country. Canada must be strong and united.
The present government will do everything to make people regain confidence in a Canada that is found neither in the state of Quebec nor in the province of Ontario but from coast to coast, from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
(Text):
As promised, one of the first acts of our Prime Minister will be to form the royal commission on biculturalism to examine, not only the past, but the present situation and report the true facts to the nation. The words unity and "biculturalism" are very important words to all Canadians. Most of us have always considered our country as one, indivisible and firm, it is important to remember that two great races, two nations, worked together to achieve that united country.
Our English speaking compatriots will remember that when our French ancestors suffered defeat at the battle of the Plains of Abraham, it was a break with their past,

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis with their traditions and their roots. Later, Quebec made a great and voluntary decision in refusing to throw in its future with what is today the United States, and made another great decision, 96 years ago, when it became part of the confederation. These were two great steps very important to the Canadians of the French heritage, and now many feel that yet another step should be taken which, in a different but equally important way, will make them a greater or more vital part of Canada's destiny. This is something to be appreciated not only by the Canadians in the brackets of high education, but by all Canadians who respect our country as a united and indivisible one.
It is important for all Canadians to study immediately our mutual problems, and this during what I call the waiting period so that those problems will not suddenly spring on all Canadians in a few years as something quite unknown to them. Such a surprise could only create unfortunate resistance. A proper presentation of Quebec's viewpoints can only be of service to our national unity.
Each day we pick up the newspapers and see large headlines, radios give us short and somewhat frightening news bulletins, and commentators review serious aspects of our national life. Sometimes it seems that matters are very black and the problems are overwhelming. The reason is that good things, good news and the wonderful aspects of life do not really make big headlines, do not make the hot news bulletins and do not provide good material for the commentators. Bad news is often big news and good news is often no news at all. This is an important thing for everyone to remember in these days, because from the Atlantic to the Pacific there are many, many happy, constructive and wonderful things happening to help our nation grow, be healthy and to develop.
Our duty and responsibility as elected representatives in the House of Commons is not only to help those constructive and pleasant aspects of life, but to go to the heart of the troubles and problems and do the best we can to cure and clear them up. To aid in embarkation upon such a course, there should be a clear statement of our views, policies and of what we are trying to do within the limitation of our responsibilities here in Ottawa, because we must not only recognize what is our duty, but also the boundaries over which we must not step so as not to offend, trespass upon or damage the spirits, acts and works of the provinces. To help mutual understanding between English and French speaking citizens in Canada we do not have

to wait until the commission on biculturalism produces its report; we can do so in great measure now.
Immediately following the recent election I took upon myself to do what I believe others should do. I went with my wife across Canada to the west coast for a journey. Our trip was an inspiration to us and I recommend it to every resident of the province of Quebec.
I remember that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) suggested we should visit western Canada, and I am happy to have done so. I have some very strong convictions and opinions on this subject. I think it is a delight to visit these places, but I, like the hon. member for Edmonton West, think also you will find it just as wonderful to know Canada better. The glories of our Pacific coast, of the breathtaking Rockies, of the cities of Vancouver, Edmonton and Calgary, the vast expanse of our prairies, and the huge inland seas of the great lakes are things that every Canadian should see.
I do not know how travelling in Canada can be encouraged more than it is now, but I do feel that our government and every provincial government should do all within their power to get Canadians to visit Canadians. While I was in Vancouver recently it was my pleasure and privilege to discuss with many people the principle of exchanging students between British Columbia and Quebec. I would welcome any suggestions on "exchange," because I feel it will not only aid the education and the culture of these young Canadians who are exchanged between Quebec and other provinces but will move us closer towards national unity. Greater understanding must be the keynote. Canadians of French lineage must deal with citizens of other provinces and exchange speakers, visitors, residents, athletes, artists, and students. By friendly persuasion and by personal contact the friendships, the viewpoints, the associations between Quebec and the other provinces will be strengthened.
Travel within Canada must be accelerated at a speed never before considered or contemplated. I am convinced that this is one of the most urgent requirements. What is the cost of this great travel? What will it cost to transport people at perhaps reduced fares, or on special scholarships from school to school, or event to event, or city to city? I venture that it will cost nothing in relation to the price of unity, for Canadian unity is beyond all price.
Many years ago when our wheat crops on the prairies were threatened with disaster from manpower shortages, it was possible to travel from Montreal to the prairies to work in the wheat fields for $25. This comes to my

mind when I think of the tremendous value now of travel from west to east, and east to west. Would it not be a wonderful thing for Montreal students to be able to view Vancouver's beauty at such a small cost for transportation, and for young westerners to brush up on their French by a visit to "la belle province" of Quebec at the same cost from their homes?
It is my feeling that a message must be directed through all possible media to all Canadians. That message should reach them by television, radio, newspapers, magazines, meetings and other means. It should communicate the very spirit of the province of Quebec, which summed up is something like this: When the 13 colonies broke away from the empire, it was the decision of the Canadians of French lineage to stay and make today's Canada possible.
(Translation):
Thereupon, Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude my remarks, and I hope that all hon. members will as best they can co-operate to make a success of this survey on biculturalism, which will take place in the near future.
I know that each hon. member has definite views and quite a few representations to make. I hope that they will play their part vigorously and sincerely and contribute to the effort of this government with a view to uniting this country for the benefit of each and every Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, next week, we will have to vote on the budget. I hope that our friends in the opposition will let us have a strong majority vote to express their confidence in the Minister of Finance, who knew how to resort to expert advice. I hope that they will also support the Minister of Finance and the party now in power so that we may take the action needed to strengthen this country, our Canada.
The other day I heard the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire)-who is unfortunately not in his seat right now-blame the Liberals for having said, during the last election, that they would find a solution for unemployment. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lapointe, who is a man in a hurry, wanted the Liberal party to settle in 60 days, in one fell swoop, the whole unemployment problem.
Well, obviously we have four years before us, and by means of the legislation we shall enact, we shall solve the unemployment problem.
Incidentally, while we are speaking of promises, the hon. member for Lapointe might
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis have remembered that, between a promise and reality there is often a difference, coming more particularly from the Social Credit side.
We promised to put an end to unemployment. We shall certainly manage to do it within four years, and we can count on that many years.
During the last session of the previous parliament, the hon. member for Lapointe predicted that the Liberals would be huddled together with the Conservatives in a little corner of this house on the left of the Speaker, while Social Crediters would be seated on his right. But, what happened actually? Exactly the opposite. Moreover, we have four years to keep our promises, but he has only four years to prevent those who stayed with him from crossing over to this side of the house.
We found, on the evening of April 8, that the Social Credit party was down to 20 members in the house, and that some time after one of them came over to this side of the house, while others shed tears and still others went their own way.
This is what the promises made by the hon. member for Lapointe brought him.
As far as I am concerned, I wish him the longest tenure in this house, because he amuses us a lot, but without any intention of disheartening him I must tell him that after the next election Social Credit will have become a thing of the past.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis). Could the hon. member tell me, for my information and for the information of the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Tremblay), if he agrees with the establishment of a department of agriculture for eastern Canada as he said this afternoon and as he repeated so many times during the last election campaign in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am most happy, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member asked that question for his information because he certainly needs information.
I say that I agree with the appointment of the present Minister without Portfolio as minister of agriculture for eastern Canada, and I can tell you that this wish will be fulfilled in a near future.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But the hon. member this afternoon stated he was in favour of the establishment of the department of agriculture. Is he in favour of the establishment of a separate department of agriculture for

The Budget-Mr. MacEwan eastern Canada or is he supporting the mere appointment of an eastern agriculture minister?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I believe my hon. friend understood perfectly that I meant both.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville?
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being the first opportunity I have had to participate in formal debate this session may I first congratulate you, sir, the Deputy Speaker, and the deputy chairman of committees who comes from the Atlantic provinces, on your election to the high offices you hold.
I listened with interest to the speech made by the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State. My speech will not be as rapid, but I note he ended his remarks with a reference to his favourite subject, the Social Credit party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It used to be my favourite subject.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I mentioned to him at one time the translation into French is not quite apt, but I understand that during the last election he out-Caouetted Caouette, and the result of that is that he is now parliamentary secretary.
As a maritimer I want to say that we in the Atlantic provinces are a little bit leery about the budget and about the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is Minister of Finance. Only time will tell, but we will watch what happens. We know the Minister of Finance visited us. We know he wrote a report. We know he was chairman of a royal commission, and on many occasions reference has been made to his remarks about mari-timers leaving the Atlantic provinces, especially coal miners in whom I am very interested.
He also said that if we in the maritimes wanted to stay there we would have to accept a standard of living lower than that in other parts of the country. I know he has since said that he really did not mean to say that. In fact he returned to my constituency some time ago and made a very good speech there, a copy of which unfortunately I left at home. However, I have little doubt he had assistance in the preparation of it from another Liberal hon. member. I am not certain, but I have been told that, and I refer to the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Even

though the minister has said he did not mean to say those things, nevertheless we will watch what happens so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned.
We in the maritimes thought we had a good set-up which would help us, in the fact that during the last session of parliament we had as minister of finance the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). He did an excellent job and we wanted to continue that. The minister of finance is a very important man in any government. In addition to that we had as the minister in charge of the Atlantic development board the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), former minister of forestry and former premier of the province of New Brunswick, who is very close to us in the maritimes.
Now we have the Secretary of State in charge of that board. He has been a representative of Newfoundland for some time, but after all he is not a native born Atlantic province member, and if we were to have a change of government I wondered if perhaps we might not have the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) or the genial Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) in charge of that board. However, the result is that we have a complete change, in a minister of finance from Ontario and a minister in charge of the Atlantic development board who is not a native born of the Atlantic provinces. We will have to watch very closely what occurs.
I should like to deal with the budget as it affects the maritimes. Resolutions have been introduced regarding the new department of industry and the area development agency that is to form part of it. I am not completely sold on this. I believe the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) dealt with this matter when he spoke on the resolution stage, and I do not intend to repeat his arguments. But in order to help labor surplus areas-and my constituency in that respect is one of the worst in Canada-I believe this further division that is proposed will not help at all, particularly with regard to my own area.
During his budget speech the minister said:
The full effect on the economy of the Important measures I have been discussing-
He was referring to the measures being introduced for the labour surplus areas.
-will not be felt for a few years.
That is not what we were told during the last election campaign. In my area the Liberal candidate said that all that had to happen was a change of government and there would immediately be no unemployment. Now the minister says the effect of these measures will not be felt for a few years.

Since 1957, many steps have been taken to help the economy of the Atlantic region. Among them were the subsidies to shipbuilding. They were important to my area and many other parts of Canada. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and hon. members from the west coast know what these subsidies meant. However, I was a little distressed when the minister had this to say about the shipbuilding subsidies-and I am not going to quote him. This is to be found on page 1002 of Hansard, for June 13:
Other matters could also be mentioned. There is the shipbuilding subsidy, which was reduced, effective last April 1, in such a way as to lead to a sudden irrational surge of expenditure and activity in that industry which is unlikely to be sustained.
Then he went on to say this:
This surge of activity places a substantial burden on this year's budget without producing any continuing benefit.
I do not know whether I agree with that. I believe that the benefits will be continuing, and I only hope, despite the words used by the minister, that there will be no move whatsoever to remove these shipbuilding subsidies. They have meant many more jobs, and the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) former minister of transport has estimated the total at 50,000. If the Minister of Finance is thinking of removing these subsidies I would ask him to check first with the Minister of Transport and the Canadian maritime commission. During the last few years many of us pressed for such subsidies in order to help our shipyards compete with foreign shipyards, and if these subsidies are taken away it will mean the loss of a great many jobs and will be a great blow to the shipbuilding industry. For that reason I hope those words used by the minister are not words of warning.
The previous administration also introduced an important measure with regard to vocational training. In fact, I believe the government I supported led by the Leader of the Opposition did more in regard to vocational training than any other government in the history of the country. I do not want to burden the house with references that are too long, but I can look back to the time when coal mines were being closed down in my area and the miners had no trade or skill to use in other work. That was a time when a very strong vocational program should have been introduced. But now I am very pleased to say that as a result of the action taken by the previous government in providing 75 per cent of the cost of vocational schools, through agreement with the provinces, a new school will open in my area in the fall. The young people who take vocational training in it, with the additional advantage of their high school
The Budget-Mr. MacEwan education, will be fine citizens and they will be equipped to stay at home and work in the area. This is something that should have been done before, but I point out that these are matters that will take a little time. The results are being felt in Canada now and, of course, hon. gentlemen across the way will probably get the credit for it.
The Atlantic development board has been referred to also and I should like to point out that the minister said that the Atlantic development board was being strengthened by setting up a fund. I am not going into that. Others of my colleagues from the Atlantic area have done so. However, I would point out that the vice-chairman of the board, Mr. Sobey, who was to sit for five years, will be gone in a year. This is not strengthening the board. This man has been president of Industrial Estates Limited, the crown company in Nova Scotia and I looked upon him as the liaison between Industrial Estates Limited and the Atlantic development board. But when the year is up I suggest that this man, regardless of politics, be re-appointed to the board. He is necessary especially for my native province of Nova Scotia.
Next week an unemployment meeting will be held in my area. Mention was made of this today and there are various things that will probably come up. A local committee has been set up to look into the matter. It is a non-political body known as the Pictou county research and development association. This association has been doing a lot of work in the last two years and carrying out research into various things. I think this will be of assistance to the area. A labour surplus area such as mine should be the first problem attacked by the Atlantic development board.
There is one matter in the budget which has been referred to by the financial editor of the Montreal Gazette and it might be worth while mentioning it here. I refer to the question of accelerated depreciation. I will not quote at length but it is a matter which was missed in the budget and it is something which should be referred to at this time. Tax incentives are good and we welcome the three year tax holiday. We also welcome accelerated depreciation but I want to point out what Mr. Meyer said on June 14:
One would wish he-
The Minister of Finance.
-might have been more imaginative. His purposes are clear enough. The increase in capital investment which the accelerated write-offs can be expected to persuade is certainly desirable but might he not be overdoing it? The problem is not entirely one of encouraging new investment; there is also the need to encourage more efficient use of existing investment.

The Budget-Mr. MacEwan
Here is the important part.
For all the pick-up in business which has taken place over the last year, idle plant can still be readily found. In a good many instances, it is the market that is lacking, not the production equipment to serve that market.
I think that is something which the minister missed, the matter of markets. There should have been something to stimulate markets not only in our country but abroad. The former government of which I was a supporter set a record in the exporting of manufactured goods to other countries through the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. They were always willing to help companies. I submit to the present government that they should go ahead on this basis. It means a lot to the manufacturers of this country. There are many areas which are open including the South American area. Let the government go ahead. Apparently they are not looking to this too much because it was not mentioned in the budget speech. I might also refer to this comment on the budget:
It offers no stimulation for exports. In fact, It could be regressive in this field because it imposes a sales tax on manufacturing machinery and will almost inevitably add to the cost of production in Canada and consequently make Canadian goods less competitive at home and abroad. Mr. Gordon has tried to do a Roman ride on horses galloping in opposite directions.
I bring this to the attention of the minister. Export markets are important to Canada and we cannot hope to use all the products that we manufacture in this country.
Going on from there, sir, may I refer to the 11 per cent sales tax. I have spoken to my colleagues on this side of the house from the Atlantic provinces, which have a very high rate of unemployment as we all know, and they tell me unequivocally that they have received many submissions on the matter of the sales tax which may be vital to many companies, especially smaller companies in our area. One thinks of the lumber firms and the contractors in their bidding. One thinks of people buying small homes and of people making repairs to their homes. The sales tax will certainly be detrimental in that regard. I know that submissions have been made to the minister from many parts of Canada and I hope that he will take them into consideration.
We have also heard about the $500 incentive with regard to the purchasing of homes. The Kingston Whig-Standard of June 15 had this to say:
With regard to the housing industry, the new budget announces the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax exemption on building materials and this appears to offset the $500 bonus. What the government has actually done is to add 4 per cent to the price of new houses by this action.


Therefore this will be a very serious matter throughout the country. Another matter has been mentioned which has been brought to the attention of members of the official opposition. In my riding there is a company which manufactures prefab houses and I know there are others throughout the country. I understand that the 11 per cent sales tax will apply on the total cost or over-all package deal with regard to prefabs. Many times prefab manufacturers, especially on the east coast and the west coast, are required to move these houses long distances. I know that from my own area many of them have been shipped north to the lake Janine and Port Cartier area, and Eskimo homes have also been shipped to the far north. This tax will add to the cost. I doubt very much that this company will be able to compete with the companies in Ontario and Quebec. This all adds up to lack of jobs.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) referred to the matter of the pegging of the Canadian dollar and I will not belabour that now. He always deals with these things very delicately and much more easily than I do. However, I know that during the June, 1962 election campaign much was made of the pegging of the Canadian dollar. I do not have the page here but I believe that the Minister of Finance said that the dollar would continue to be pegged because it had been helpful especially with regard to exports. We know that in our own province products such as fish and lumber have been stimulated by the pegging of the dollar, and now the truth will indeed be told.
There are other matters in the budget I could go into but I do not intend to repeat what other speakers have said. May I end by repeating that as members from the Atlantic area and representatives of the people of that region we are watching the Minister of Finance. The minister said that if the tax holiday did not help the Atlantic provinces he did not know what would. He had other things to say originally about that area because at one time he thought it would help to move people from Cape Breton and my area. He put forward various things but now he thinks that this tax write-off will help us and he said that if it did not do so he did not know what would.
As was pointed out by my hon. member for Cape Breton South, anything that stimulates the Atlantic area will help the rest of Canada. Certainly we do not intend to be the doomsters and gloomsters that members of the former opposition were. If this will help, and this was said by my colleague also, we will certainly be pleased but it will definitely have to be proven to us.

Finally, sir, in so far as outside people assisting in the preparation of the budget is concerned, that is a matter with which I am not going to deal. It has been dealt with by other members. The same is true of the withdrawal of the 30 per cent tax on stocks. The people of Canada, as well as the people in the Atlantic area, are disturbed today. I should like to conclude by again referring to the Montreal Gazette in which there was this article by Mr. Meyer:
What is so disturbing here is that Mr. Gordon's bungling has cast an early pall over the initially successfully efforts of the new government to clean up the smudges put upon Canada's image abroad by the previous government.
I am not accepting that.
Few governments have entered office with such sincere foreign good wishes-sentiments which were admirably justified by Mr. Pearson's appearance in London and Hyannis Port and Mr. Sharp's hard-headedness at Geneva. The budget, which should have put a capstone to these efforts to rebuild foreign confidence instead brought the whole structure tumbling down.
We accept the budget, therefore, as it is. We are watching to see whether or not it will bring about the solution of the unemployment problem in Canada to which reference was made by the previous speaker. We do not believe it will. If it will help out, we will buy it. We will see how these people who sit in their ivory towers bring about full employment in this country. We do not believe they can. We will be watching them closely during the days and months ahead.

Which are; this, at least, would be agreed by all hon. members, that certain facets of the Canadian economy need to be strengthened and certain of our industries stimulated and made more efficient if we are going to overcome some of the basic difficulties with which we are confronted.
Perhaps I might just remind hon. members what these basic difficulties are. In the first place, there is no disagreement in this house, I think, that unemployment is a scourge; that it works not only a great hardship on the people concerned but it is a source of fear to others who are afraid that they, too, may lose
Private Bills
their jobs. We have to do something about this in Canada. We must tackle it, it seems to me, on a variety of levels. We must, if we are going to be successful, look at the long term as well as the short term. I do not believe, myself, that merely dealing with the short term problems as they arise will work in this field or any other. It was for that reason-it is for that reason-that we on this side of the house attach so much importance to the work of the proposed department of industry. This department, working with the industries concerned, and as I have said before, working with the trade unions concerned, will be responsible for bringing about some major reorganization of the industrial structure of this country. It will take time, working at it one industry at a time, if our industries are to become strong enough to compete with competitors from abroad and if they are to be in a position to expand their exports. When I say that I am thinking of manufactured goods as well as primary products.
Now, I do not think there is much disagreement either that our balance of payments problem, the imbalance in our current accounts which has been running at the rate of about a billion dollars a year, is at the root of many of the problems that we face in Canada. I think the year before it was a little less. Several hon. members have discussed very helpfully and well some aspects of our economic problem. I hope that during the remainder of this debate many hon. members will focus their attention on this particular aspect of the problem, this imbalance in our current account transactions, and will say what they think should be done about it. As I said, 1 believe this is at the root of our problem and is one of the reasons we have had so much unemployment in this country in recent years.
May I call it five o'clock?
