subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ADD REMEMBRANCE DAY AS HOLIDAY

speakeroldname: Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ADD REMEMBRANCE DAY AS HOLIDAY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-13, to amend the Civil Service Act (Remembrance day).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill reflects the feelings of the members of the Royal Canadian Legion, other veterans groups in Canada, relatives of veterans and many other Canadians with respect to the recognition of remembrance day.
Before dealing with the content of my bill I wish to give a brief historical review of the legislation with respect to the recognition of what was first termed armistice day and later remembrance day, November 11, a never to be forgotten day by veterans of the first world war and their relatives, who will always remember the great sigh of relief that was raised throughout the world when that war terminated. I find the first reference to recognition of this day was during 1919, and I quote from Hansard of May 23, 1921, when a Mr. Pedlow speaking in this house said:
In the first session of 1919, that which immediately followed the cessation of hostilities, I proposed the following resolution, which appears as No. 37 on page 25 of the order paper of Monday, April 7.
This was the resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, November 11 of each year should be set aside as a day of national thanksgiving, to be a perpetual memorial to the signing of the armistice, ending the great world war.
Then Mr. Pedlow went on to say:
Almost immediately after that resolution appeared on the order paper the press of Canada from one end of the country to the other commented favourably on the proposal.
I find that the matter was discussed in the house and mentioned on numerous occasions. Then an act respecting armistice day was assented to on June 4, 1921. It is quite obvious that there has been a change of approach to November 11 throughout the years. First of all the speeches made in this house and the legislation enacted generally

expressed a spirit of thanksgiving for the termination of the first world war. Then later, as the war became more distant, we see that replaced by a desire for remembrance of the services of those who served in that and more recent wars. That is indicated in this legislation and I will quote two sections of an act respecting armistice day, chapter 16. Section 2 reads:
Throughout Canada in each and every year the Monday in the week in which the eleventh day of November shall occur being the day in 1918 in which the great war was triumphantly concluded by an armistice, shall be a legal holiday and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of armistice day.
It goes on to say in section 3:
The holiday commonly called thanksgiving day being a day usually appointed in the month of October or November by proclamation as a day of general thanksgiving to Almighty God, shall whenever appointed be proclaimed and observed for and on armistice day.
I mention those two sections of this act, Mr. Speaker, because they illustrate the general, shall I say, spirit of thanksgiving with which the recognition of this day was approached at that time. Then we find that the approach changes to one of remembrance of the services performed by those who served in the first world war, those who lost their loved ones, and so on. So we have the Remembrance Day Act passed in 1931, which declared that November 11 would always be recognized as remembrance day. Later we find references to this in the Civil Service Act of 1931, with which I shall deal later. Throughout the years there has been a general feeling on the part of many members of veterans organizations and other Canadians that there is not in this country sufficient recognition of remembrance day; that people in some cases are more concerned with holidays as such rather than with recognizing a day in remembrance of the services performed by those who served in the armed forces, and others, in the first and second world wars and the Korean war. Those feelings found expression in Legion conventions, particularly the last two or three dominion conventions of the Royal Canadian Legion. There has been considerable discussion on this subject. As a matter of fact, at the present time a committee of the national council of the Royal Canadian Legion is giving serious consideration to several aspects of the better recognition by Canadians of remembrance day. I wish to quote the two resolutions that were dealt with at the last convention of the Royal Canadian Legion with respect to the recognition of remembrance day:

Whereas there is a growing tendency across Canada to treat November 11 as just another holiday rather than a day sacred to the memory of our fallen comrades, and
Whereas the government of Canada saw fit to grant the civil service a holiday on an alternate date when November 11 fell on a Saturday or Sunday:
Therefore be it resolved that the Royal Canadian Legion informed the government that its action in this regard is deplored and that the legion looks to the government to set an example to the significance of remembrance day.
There was a second resolution. I will quote it because I want to place before the house the attitude of the members of the Royal Canadian Legion in dominion convention assembled:
Whereas the 11th of November each year has been established as the day to pay respect and to remember comrades who made the supreme sacrifice, and
Whereas in many cities and towns business continues to be carried on as usual all during remembrance day, thus affording the staffs no opportunity to pay respect to the fallen:
Therefore be it resolved that dominion and provincial governments again be requested to declare November 11 a statutory holiday so that every person not engaged in essential services will have an opportunity to attend remembrance day services.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the reason for my introducing this bill. I want to give some explanation of the purpose of this bill, which is in line with the sentiments expressed at conventions of the Royal Canadian Legion. The purpose of this bill is to restore, in so far as the parliament of Canada is legislatively able, remembrance day to the position intended by the spirit and meaning of the Remembrance Day Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 237. That act provides:
Throughout Canada in each and every year, the 11th day of November, being the day in the year 1918 on which the great war was triumphantly concluded by an armistice, shall be a holiday, and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of remembrance day.
The Civil Service Act chapter 57 section 62 provides that remembrance day shall be a holiday for the civil service for which leave of absence may be substituted if it falls on a day when civil servants are not required to work. However, the section limits the holiday to civil servants and presumably leaves the declaration of the holiday, if it is one in the public service, to the discretion of the responsible crown authority. This bill uses the term "public service" which would include all those employed in crown corporations and similar establishments.
In clause 1 of this bill, remembrance day is deleted from the list of holidays in subsection (1) for which leave of absence may be substituted under subsection (2). Subsection (3) is added so that remembrance day becomes a holiday in the language and within
Civil Service Act
the meaning of the Remembrance Day Act. The wider meaning of public service is substituted for "civil service" so that government boards, commissions and agencies are included. I should like to point out that the present Civil Service Act, the sections dealing with this question, do not square with the provisions of the Remembrance Day Act. This bill is an attempt to restore the spirit and the purpose of the Remembrance Day Act as originally designed and intended.
I have mentioned that in the early days there was a general spirit of thanksgiving. The farther we get away from the first world war, the second world war and the Korean war, the more people look to November 11 as a day of remembrance upon which they have the opportunity to pay tribute to those who gave their lives, or sacrificed, or lost relatives in the defence of our country and in the defence of principles in which we all believe.
I fully realize there may be differences of opinion with respect to this amending bill. I have expressed the point of view of the Royal Canadian Legion and other organizations, and I may say it is my personal viewpoint. I have a particular interest in the recognition of remembrance day because my father, my wife and three of my family served this country in war and because I happen to be the president of the 54th Kootenay battalion association which is very keen on having this subject considered in the house. I know there are a good many others here who take the same attitude as I do. We have another generation growing up in Canada and we have many new citizens coming to this country who are, naturally, not well informed as to what these fellow citizens of ours did for Canada in two world wars and in the Korean war.
I fully realize that this is a subject which should be given every consideration so that all points of view can be heard. Therefore, I suggest that the subject matter of this bill should be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs so that the views of the Royal Canadian Legion, widows organizations, veterans organizations and other organizations particularly interested in the wider recognition of remembrance day, might be heard. There would also be an opportunity to hear the views of representatives of the civil service organizations. I realize that at the present time discussions are going on with respect to the relationship between the civil service and the federal government-discussions concerning bargaining rights and so on. This subject would, I am sure, come within the compass of those matters which interest

Civil Service Act
the civil service organizations. It is in recognition of the feelings of members of the veterans organizations I have mentioned, as well as of many other Canadians, that I have introduced this bill.
I do not intend to speak at greater length because I would like to hear the views of other hon. members on this subject. I think it is something of a relief on occasions in this house to have an opportunity to speak on other than strictly economic matters. I am one of those who believe that no nation grows great as a result of its sole concern for material things. There are values greater than that. I think the recognition of remembrance day is one action on the part of Canadians which could demonstrate to the world that we recognize the things of the spirit as coming first.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ADD REMEMBRANCE DAY AS HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would say, first of all, that it is one of the wonderful things about our system that the hon. member who proposed this bill should be one who has spoken in this house this session on so many occasions when we who sit on this side have found little in his observations with which we could agree, particularly when he has concerned himself with the field of economic theory. Yet on an occasion such as this I doubt very much whether there is a single member on this side of the house or, indeed, in any part of the house, who could possibly disagree with a single word the hon. member has said.
As early as 1871, Joseph Howe, speaking at South Framingham, Massachusetts, uttered these memorable words:
A wise nation preserves its records, gathers up its monuments, decorates the tombs ot its illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures and fosters national pride and love of country by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past.
I suggest that these words, two brief sentences in a long discourse, might be taken seriously by us today. We sit here in this chamber from day to day, and on hearing the debates, on hearing the acrimony, the vituperation which crosses this floor from time to time, and on seeing how petty, trivial matters seem to be the most important concern of this house from day to day rather than the important question of what we can do, collectively, to try to find solutions to the great problems facing us, such as unemployment, we may well be inclined to despair. Instead of doing the great things that we have to do, as apparently we are able in times of great national crisis, it seems that when times revert to so-called normal, we in this house, in any event, concern ourselves more with the petty and with the trivial than with the real tasks we were sent here to perform. I often

think, sitting here as a new member of this house, what somebody from another world would think if he descended here and were told: "This is where the business of this country is carried on, and carried on in this fashion and in this manner". I have the same thoughts when standing on the floor of a stock exchange, a place to which reference has been so prevalent in our discussions here during the past few days, where everyone is rushing around and roaring about. And for what purpose? Someone from another world cannot possibly decipher. In some ways I think we in this house have been carrying on our business of late in much the same manner.
It is appropriate and apropos that a bill of this kind, even though it be a private member's bill, be brought up at this time, because it may to some degree recall to us the importance of being a member of this house; the great traditions that are our heritage and that we are here not only to defend but to improve and build upon; to uphold those words which are spoken so often and lived up to so little, that the sacrifices of those who went before us would not have been in vain. I think perhaps that sometimes the game becomes bigger than the end. The winning is the important thing rather than the doing. In the game of political ins and outs, of political musical chairs, having the chair seems sometimes to be more important than doing the job. It may be that the hon. member who has presented this bill may make a few of us here at this late hour on Friday night just pause for a moment and think whether we in this house are fulfilling in the past few weeks the great traditions and expectations which those who came before us would have of us. I quote, Mr. Speaker, from the tablet in the memorial chamber upstairs, which reads as follows:
Read how free men throughout this land kept faith in the hour of trial, and in the day of battle, remembering the traditions they had been taught, counting life nothing without liberty.
The thought I should like to express, Mr. Speaker, is that in that same memorial chamber are found these words:
Ceux qui pieusement sont morts pour la patrie, Ont le droit qu'fi leur cercueil, la foule vienne et prie. Entre les plus beaux noms, leur nom est le plus beau. La voix d'un peuple entier les berce en leur tombeau.
In this house, Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great deal about one of our fundamental problems in this nation, namely the question of biculturalism and bilingualism. Here are the roots of the very matter, the subject of this bill: A real and permanent bicultural and bilingual land. I think those who served in the armed forces during the war found almost inevitably young men and women of

French origin serving side by side, sharing danger equally, with those of us of Anglo-Saxon origin. And there were others of Irish, German, Polish and other origins who served just as well. In those days nobody asked: "What is your native tongue? What religion are you?" The issues in this matter did not occur to anyone. The only thing that mattered was the job on hand; what we could do for our country together at that time.
If we recall these last two wars we will find we had a very great foundation of a bilingual nation; for a nation which was truly bicultural. Those of us who served in the air force, as I did, often discussed the fact that while there was criticism at home about the service of French Canadians during the war, it is the fact and statistics indicate that over 50 per cent of those who enlisted in air crew, which possibly was the highest casualty area of the war, were casualties and that very many of these were of French Canadian origin. So that those of us who served in air crew in the R.C.A.F. had no doubts whatsoever that our French Canadian friends and brethren played a full and responsible part with the rest of Canada. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, if we remember the admonition of Mr. Howe to honour our past, to refurbish our monuments and to build upon our great foundations, I think we have a very fine start for this young nation, as we still are, to become a great bilingual and bicultural nation.
The bill is intended primarily, as I read it, to create a holiday for persons in the civil service on remembrance day. As my hon. friend from across the floor suggested, the important thing is not so much the holiday but the remembrance which should be stressed on this particular day. I was most interested, in doing research on this bill, to discover that in 1921, when the bill concerning armistice day was originally presented, these words were said in this house, as reported on page 3773 of Hansard for that year:
Mr. Chairman, I thought this bill was originally introduced by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow).
I am pleased to see that as the hon. member for Renfrew South I stand here in an honoured tradition in speaking on this bill which was originally introduced by Mr. Pedlow, the hon. member for South Renfrew at that time. I noted with some concern that at that time, during a brief respite which this party does have from time to time, he was in opposition.
I should also like to refer to a further debate which took place in 1931 when the bill was revised in its present form. I think the gist of the revision was that it segregated
Civil Service Act
thanksgiving day and armistice day, which used to be celebrated together. Some of the words spoken by Mr. Geary, the then hon. member for South Toronto, are pertinent and should commend themselves to our consideration. He said, as reported on page 1062 of 1931 Hansard:
The 11th of November is an appropriate day for that purpose. Thus far we have celebrated Armistice day on November 11 throughout the country. I cannot speak of other parts of Canada than my own home, but there, at eleven o'clock on the morning of November 11, we have a service which is attended by thousands upon thousands of people. Not only is that service attended by these thousands of people, all apparently devout, all very lovingly commemorating the men who lost their lives in the war, but at eleven o'clock as if by common consent, throughout the whole city, in transportation activities, in industrial enterprises, in the shops, on the street, in the courts, everywhere, all activities cease for the short space of two minutes. Men go about their business afterwards but they do not lose the refreshment of memory which they have derived from that one simple act. If this day, through being made a holiday, degenerate into something that has not as its foremost and practically exclusive function this perpetuation of the memories of these men, I think we should be losing all that is sweet, all that is fine in the observances of the occasion.
I think my hon. friend stressed this point, and I think it should be stressed very strongly, that this should not be just a holiday. It should be an occasion not merely when we remember those who fell in the two world wars, but when we should rededicate ourselves to make this country and this land a little more like the place they would have liked to see if they were still here.
To that end may I introduce a suggestion at this time. I understand this bill is going to the committee and I suggest that November 11 should be celebrated in such manner that the provisions of the Lord's Day Act would be made applicable to it. Would it not be possible, instead of November 11 merely being a holiday when we can do whatever we want, when the Coney islands of our country are opened up and when our theatres are opened up, that it be made more than just a holiday and that the Lord's Day Act be applied to November 11?
When the bill goes to the committee I hope the committee will do a little more than just consider it. It is my hope that the entire veterans charter, which I am very proud to say is the product of this party, will be reviewed in that committee in the light of present day needs and circumstances, and in the light of the value of the dollar today as compared with the value of the dollar at the time when many of the rates were set up under the veterans charter.
I think we all owe, not only in this house but in the country, a very great debt of

Civil Service Act
gratitude to organizations such as the Canadian Legion, the air force association and similar veterans organizations that have made it their job to see that those men and women who served their country are not forgotten. In this day of government to so large a degree by public opinion, it is essential that these people have organizations to speak for them in a corporate way. If they were left to their individual resources I am sure their lot would not be as good today as it is, thanks to the work of the Canadian Legion and similar organizations.
I suggest many of the beneficiaries under veterans' legislation, in particular those persons receiving war veterans' allowances, are in very grave need of consideration today. I think that the return they are getting today is scarcely enough to keep body and soul together. I suggest when this bill goes to the committee there should be a revision of the entire veterans' charter, of the needs of the men and women who served in our armed forces, and in particular of the needs and requirements of those men and women who, today, are disabled by age or by wounds or otherwise from sharing the fruits of the economy of this thriving country. We, the rest of us who are whole, hale and hearty would be only too glad to play our part and to sacrifice a little if we have to, in order to see that these good men and women who did so much for us will not live in penury but will be able to live in dignity and be able to share in some fair measure in the bounties of this land.
I am very pleased to support my hon. friend's bill, strange as this may be, as we are on opposite sides of the house, and I hope when the bill goes to committee the general thought behind it will come to fruition, and in particular the aspect of the bill which refers to remembrance which encourages us-as Joseph Howe has said-to look at our monuments, to shine them up, and to look back so that once again we can look ahead; and that in that committee the entire position of the disabled veterans and those dependant on us by virtue of their service to the country in two world wars will be looked through carefully so that we may not break the faith with them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words but not to do my share in talking out another bill that will be dead around six o'clock. However, I feel I should make a few remarks with regard to Bill C-13.
I congratulate the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who remembered to

submit the views of the Canadian Legion and the various veterans' organizations.
I am of the opinion that the member for Kootenay West was right in insisting that throughout Canada, the 11th of November should be better observed. That is why I wish to point out that when he says:
The wider meaning of "public service"
should be used, I feel he is right. However, something seems to be lost on the house and I am surprised that the member for Kootenay West who, as a rule, is so precise and clear in his remarks, does not seem to have noticed it, particularly when my colleague, who spoke just before me, said that there is some talk of stipulating a statutory holiday to that effect.
I think that it is wrong and I believe that on that point my colleague from Kootenay West is greatly mistaken.
The Remembrance Day Act provides, as mentioned in the bill:
Throughout Canada in each and every year, the llth day of November, being the day in the year 1918 on which the great war was triumphantly concluded by an armistice, shall be a holiday, and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of remembrance day.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that on that point there is no doubt. The llth of November is already a holiday. Then what is exactly the purpose of the bill we are considering today?
It is this. Under this bill remembrance day is removed from the list of holidays so that if, at a certain time, it fell on a Saturday or a Sunday, the civil servants could not get a holiday on the next day.
I think that is the exact purpose of this bill. And I do not see how the house can agree about that. In fact, November 11 is a legal holiday whether it falls on a Monday, a Tuesday, a Saturday or a Sunday, and remembrance day must be kept as a holiday throughout Canada.
I think it is very well to seek a way of celebrating remembrance day in a more suitable way by drawing the Canadians attention to it. But if this is a means of taking away a holiday from civil servants when Remembrance Day falls on a Saturday, in order to be agreeable to the Canadian Legion and to the veterans, we do not agree on the matter.
In my opinion, this is a good bill. We should insist on the better observation of this day. But why abolish, for civil servants, the holiday which follows remembrance day when November 11 falls on a Saturday or on a Sunday? I object then to that part of the bill. Our civil servants, who do not have so many holidays during the year, must retain this one.

It has been said a while ago that it is very well to go to cemeteries and think of our departed ones at that time of the year. Well, precisely, our civil servants, who normally have only their week ends to take care of their families and house chores, are very much in favour of a possible postponement of that holiday for a day or two when it falls on a Saturday or a Sunday, so that they too may go and pray on the graves of their departed ones.
In my opinion, we should be against this bill in its present form as it would deprive civil servants of a possible holiday whereas its object is to give more importance to remembrance day.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak briefly on this bill I too would congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who has shown an interest in this subject over many years. The hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) referred to a distinguished representative of his riding who had something to say about the early legislation on this matter, and I was reminded of comments made by the gentleman who gave his name to the city where I live, General Sir Isaac Brock, one of the great Canadian veterans who, speaking in the Upper Canada legislature on July 27, 1812, said:
We are engaged in an awful and eventful contest. By unanimity and dispatch in our councils and by vigour in our operations, we will teach the enemy this lesson: that a country defended by free men, enthusiastically devoted to the cause of their king and constitution, can never be conquered.
It is strange that just as I came across this I received at the same time an invitation to be present at a large veterans gathering.of servicemen from Ontario and New York state where they are celebrating their remembrance very shortly together.
I think it is well said that periodically we should have a moment to pause in our deliberations, which are largely directed to economic considerations, in order to consider something of those things which have been referred to as being of the spirit. When we think of what has been the concern of veterans over the centuries we remember that portion of the church of England prayer book where the priest says, "Give peace in our time O Lord". This actually goes back to the time when my ancestors who were from the Scandinavian Norseland were ravaging

Anglo-Saxon England, and the reply of the congregation, many of them battle weary, was:
Because there is none other that tightest for us, but only Thou, O God.
It was a petition, almost a despairing cry, and in these happier days when the matters that are uppermost in our minds are not matters so much of war and peace, surely it is most important that we keep in mind those people who have fought for this country and who have died that we may live in the dignity that we do.
After every great war men have heard the quiet voices of the dead amid the surrounding clamour whispering a prayer for the peace of the world they died to save. Brockington of Canada, this noble voice of so many of our aspirations and hopes, speaks of the brotherhood of the brave. At one time he said:
Now what manner of men were they? They were bone of our bone, blood of our blood, the gold of our rocks, the salt of our beloved earth. The colours of their individual characters were as varied as the maple trees in the glowing of our autumn. But this was the pattern of their fibre. They all loved peace and hated the cruel necessities of war. They were kind to little children-even to the children of their enemies.
My friend who just spoke referred to some of his friends in air crew and this reminds me of the fact that the cuff links I wear were given to me by Brigadier Paul Triquet, who was a companion many years ago. His gallant men so frequently were the closest people on earth at that time to me. Only at great cost to ourselves can we forget those of them who are dead.
I think that the member who has had the foresight and concern to bring forward this legislation is seeking to change this remembrance day from one merely of merriment and perhaps casual refreshment to one where we are actually brought back even for a short while, even for a short period of hours or minutes, to what this day actually means. He referred to the resolution passed by the Royal Canadian Legion in Halifax in 1962. I have read that resolution carefully. I think the important words in it are to the effect that "the Legion looks to the government to set an example to the whole nation of the significance of remembrance day." As the hon. member said, another resolution was brought forward which provided that every person engaged in essential services should have an opportunity to attend a remembrance day service.
I am not sure whether or not the bill in its present form is exactly what those people who have studied the matter over many years would wish. I rather suspect that the Royal Canadian Legion, which at the present time is our best channel of communication

on this subject, has been exposed to two almost diametrically opposed views, but in any event I think that the bill should be considered carefully by the veterans affairs committee because it points up the fact that at the present time the day is tending to become simply a statutory holiday without the significance that we would wish it to have.
Elsewhere in his comments to the people of Canada Leonard Brockington spoke about the old play, "The Bluebird". You may remember that it was a story of children who were seeking to find the bluebird, the bluebird that in fact turned out to be the blackbird in the wicker cage in the kitchen, but they did not know it. This is a lovely story, and as the children entered the land of memory one of them said to her who was guiding them:
How can we see them when they are dead?
And she answered:
How can they be dead when they live in your memory?
Having been to a good number of school occasions where young people have been compelled as a matter of routine to observe remembrance day, I am satisfied that young people do care when somebody who is a little older takes the time to talk to them quietly and earnestly, because after all most of these people, this rich legacy of dead in the wars of Canada, were young people, young in heart, the brave and the young and the fresh. The tragedy is that as we sit even in this august chamber we lose something of that freshness, that cleanness and that spirit of dedication that they had.
There is a story about the meditation room in a British aircraft carrier during the second world war. In this place of worship there was, of course, a picture of the holy family, a Bible and certain religious relics. But there were also a number of paintings of England. A stranger who was visiting the ship went into this room and he looked around and said, "I do not really see the propriety of these pictures of England on this altar". The captain of the ship said, "Sir, when you are fighting for England every picture of England is sacred also".
I think that is very much how our sons felt about Canada, those people who would have liked to come back here and have had children, who would have liked to have businesses, farms, fishing boats and the ordinary joys. They would have liked to serve Canada in this place had the opportunity been theirs. I think that if we do anything other than remember these people in the most dignified and earnest way we can we are letting down not them but us. In Coriolanus
[Mr. Matheson.l
Shakespeare says that "Ingratitude is monstrous, and for the multitude to be ungrateful were to make a monster of the multitude".
So, Mr. Speaker, with all others who have spoken I commend our old friend from Kootenay West who so often says these things better than we can ourselves. I take my seat now in order that the government may have the opportunity to dispose of this bill in the fashion that has been indicated by previous speakers.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ADD REMEMBRANCE DAY AS HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Postmaster General:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Since it is now eight minutes to six, I wonder if I could suggest that it would be most unfair to any hon. member to start a debate on a private bill at this late time. I believe it would be the view of the house that, by unanimous consent, Mr. Speaker, you could call it six o'clock.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: There is just one comment I might make, and at least one other member who is present will confirm what I say. There was a meeting of the party representatives with the Secretary of State a few minutes ago. I believe he intends to make an announcement to the house about the business for the next number of days. Perhaps we might contain ourselves, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare would say, until the Secretary of State arrives.

Perhaps it would be appropriate if we were to exercise some patience to see if an opportunity would not present itself for us to hear from the Secretary of State. I take this opportunity of joining with other hon. members in considering the matter of deferring the debate on private bills. It is rather relaxing for those of us who come from the maritime provinces to take advantage of this opportunity. We might take advantage of it. However, I understand the Secretary of State has now arrived.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Now that the Secretary of State has returned and the government will not collapse, as he suggested to us the other day, we are waiting to hear from him with regard to the forecast of the business for the next few days and an announcement as to whether or not the house will be sitting on July 1.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the clock does not indicate six o'clock, and I am a little unaware of what has happened. However, I apologize for not being in my seat. The business for the first part of next week has already been prescribed, that is up until Wednesday night, unless after the vote on Monday hon. members feel inclined to decide that the budget has been debated long enough and allow the main motion to pass.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There may be dissolution.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps I might use the words of a very great Canadian who sat in this house for many years and say, if we are spared, when the budget debate is concluded, the first item the government would like to call is the department of industry bill, to be followed by the resolution on the Atlantic development board. I believe the debate on that is just about concluded. If we could conclude those two items on Thursday and the Atlantic board bill had been introduced on Thursday and hon. members were agreeable, we would take it on Friday. Of course, if we do not get the resolution through, we could not take the bill on Friday. The third item of business would be the economic council, subject to a matter about which I spoke to the representatives of the other parties with respect to one item on the order paper about which there may be some obligation on the government and the house to take some action. I am looking into that point.
It is felt by the government, and I think it will probably be felt by most hon. mem-
Business of the House bers that in view of the great amount of business there is to be done, we could show our respect for our country best on July 1 by getting on with the country's business, and that is what we would propose to do. I think the Minister of Finance will move on Monday, July 1, to go into committee of supply. We feel we should not go any longer without getting some of the departments entered so we can get on with the estimates.

I know the words the hon. member used are almost identical to the ones I have heard used when I sat on the other side of the house, but I think there has been a practice to adjourn for the evening of July 1 if the house would ordinarily be sitting. I think July 1 is on a Monday. I wondered if consideration had been given to that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would be glad to consider that, particularly since it will be a supply motion; if the opposition would be agreeable to adjourning that evening of July 1,1 imagine there would be no objection from this side.
There is some sort of celebration on the lawn in which everyone is supposed to join; I do not know what it is.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am perfectly happy to give consideration to that suggestion.
The mere fact I suggested it does not mean I will acquiesce.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, June 24, 1963
